summary: The compounding rule (`if (body && quantMax >= MIN_COMPOUNDING_REPEAT) return false`) is unconditional on the group body, so it refuses the canonical hierarchical-topic idiom `X+(?:sepX+)*` — a decomposition that is provably unique and linear because each repetition is forced to begin (or end) with a mandatory separator the inner quantifier's charset cannot consume. isRedosSafeSource's own JSDoc says the screen is "deliberately stricter than necessary; a legitimate topic pattern is nowhere near either bound", which is false for the most common shape an operator will write. The 15-row SAFE_PATTERNS corpus in src/testing/regex-corpus.ts contains no row of this shape, and regex-safety.test.ts grades only the leak direction (40k+ generated sources, all timed for accepted ones), so nothing in the suite can see it.
failure: `post_topics: ["[a-z]+(?:-[a-z]+)*"]` -> parseConfig throws at path post_topics.0 with "pattern risks catastrophic backtracking (a repeatable ambiguous group ...); a caller-supplied topic could hang the bridge. Simplify it." Measured: `^(?:[a-z]+(?:-[a-z]+)*)$` matches a 64-char worst-case input in 0.01 ms. Same refusal for `(?:[a-z]+\.)*[a-z]+` (0.01 ms), `[a-z0-9]+(?:/[a-z0-9]+)+` (0.02 ms), `ctx-(?:[a-z]+-)*[0-9]+`, `[a-z]+(?:_[a-z]+){0,3}` (a bounded 0..3 repeat), `team-[a-z]{2,8}(?:-[a-z]{2,8})*`. 7 of 8 idiomatic patterns probed were refused; the diagnosis in the message is wrong for every one.
remediation: Exempt a GUARDED repeat from the compounding rule while leaving the ambiguity budget in force: when the quantified group's body contains no top-level `|` and begins (or ends) with a mandatory single-character atom — a literal, an escaped literal or a character class — whose character set is disjoint from the set every quantifier inside that body can consume, do not return false; charge repetitionCost as usual. Requires tracking, per group, the leading/trailing mandatory atom and the union of quantified atoms' charsets; keep the rule conservative (bail out to the current refusal whenever a nested group or an alternation makes either set unknown).
testUpgrade: Add a SAFE_PATTERNS family to src/testing/regex-corpus.ts parameterised over separator x position x quantifier-form — `sep` in {-, _, /, ., ::}, position in {leading, trailing}, form in {*, +, {0,3}, {1,4}} — each row asserted accepted at all three entry points by regex-screen-parity.test.ts AND timed under PER_MATCH_BUDGET_MS by regex-safety.test.ts, plus the paired UNGUARDED negatives (`(?:-[a-z-]+)*`, `(?:a[abc]*)*`) that must stay refused because the separator is inside the inner charset. Widen regex-safety.test.ts's contract from "accepted implies bounded" to a two-sided one: every generated source whose wrapped regex resolves under 1 ms on all inputsFor() and which contains no nested unbounded quantifier over an unguarded body must be ACCEPTED — that turns the whole 40k generator into a false-positive detector as well as a leak detector.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: regex-safety.ts's existing `)` handler, specifically the `const body = ambiguous.pop() ?? false;` / `if (body && quantMax >= MIN_COMPOUNDING_REPEAT) return false;` branch, and the `charge(branchCount)` / `charge(repetitionCost(...))` lines that must still run for an exempted group so MAX_AMBIGUITY keeps bounding it.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `[a-z]+(?:-[a-z]+)*` (and `(?:[a-z]+\.)*[a-z]+`, `[a-z0-9]+(?:/[a-z0-9]+)+`), all of which parseConfig and the Allowlist constructor reject today.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — the exemption only removes a refusal; the ambiguity budget and every other refusal path are untouched.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I checked the four AMBIGUOUS_BODIES rows in regex-safety.test.ts's pivot sweep ('a|aa', '[a-z]*[a-z]*[a-z]*[a-z]*', 'a?', '[a-z]+') — none has a mandatory leading/trailing atom disjoint from its inner quantifier charset, and 'a|aa' is excluded by the no-top-level-alternation clause, so all 24 CELLS keep their current verdict; and all 20 HOSTILE_PATTERNS rows in src/testing/regex-corpus.ts, none of which has a guarded body. I did not run the suite against an implemented fix, so this is reasoning over the corpora, not an observed green.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied and the analysis is wrong for some body shape, a genuinely ambiguous repeat becomes accepted and Allowlist.has can be driven into exponential backtracking by a caller-supplied topic of up to 64 characters — strictly worse than the usability defect it closes. That is why the exemption must bail out to the current refusal on any nested group or alternation rather than trying to compute a charset through them.

summary: The MEASUREMENT lint is documented as guarding the CLASS CLAUDE.md names ("what a number was measured at belongs in the commit message") and ships a `fires`/`passes` control pair that makes it read as covered, but the matcher is keyed to three exact phrasings. Four live violations in this repository walk past it under a green suite, one of them in this package's own scope. Unlike the sibling lints, whose subjects are derived (the backend roster from the manifests, the file universe from `workspaces`), this rule's SUBJECT — how a measurement can be phrased — is a hand-written literal, which is the decay mode the file's own comments warn about for the universe half.
failure: `packages/bridge-core/src/regex-safety.test.ts:455` reads `// calibration with no aggregate at all (64 copies of WORST cost 34 ms, 20 000 cost 7.5 s of blocked` — a number a machine once produced, in a comment. `MEASUREMENT.test('64 copies of WORST cost 34 ms')` is `false`, so `it('no comment or test name quotes a measurement')` reports zero offenders. Same for `src/engine/presence.test.ts:570` ("the cell that costs 49 s"), `:734` ("the real wiring took 49 s"), `:1082` ("costs ~9ms against 64 characters, 1.7s").
remediation: Make the matcher shape-keyed rather than phrase-keyed: flag any commentary line where a bare numeral is adjacent to a time or size unit inside a past/observational verb frame — e.g. `/\b(?:was measured|benchmarked|measured|cost|costs|took|takes|ran in|runs in|finishes in|spends?)\b[^.]{0,40}?\d[\d,.]*\s*(?:ns|us|µs|ms|s|sec|seconds?|minutes?|[KMG]?B)\b/i`, with the existing `passes` rows kept as the false-positive controls and the four current violations rewritten as bounds ("the aggregate is bounded by MAX_POST_TOPICS x the per-source budget") or moved to the commit message.
testUpgrade: Give every LINT a MUTATION column alongside `fires`/`passes`: a list of REPHRASINGS of each `fires` string that must also fire ("cost 34 ms", "took 49 s", "runs in 9ms", "benchmarked at 12 ms"), generated from a verb x unit x tense table rather than hand-listed, so a matcher narrower than its own advice line fails as a missing row. Pair it with a rule that the offender scan is run over the repo BEFORE the rephrasings are added, so the table cannot be tuned to the repository's current text. The existing `it('the rule "quotes a measurement" fires on %j')` rows are too narrow to catch this because every row is a phrase the regex was written from.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: source-hygiene.test.ts's `commentaryLines()` (which already puts these lines in scope — I verified the offending text is inside a `//` comment and is not blanked by the STRINGS pass) and the `it.each(LINTS.map(...))('no comment or test name %s')` offender loop.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — the widened matcher only adds refusals.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: the four listed comment lines, plus any future comment pairing an observational verb with a number and a unit.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: `it('the rule "quotes a measurement" leaves %j alone')` for the row 'the budget is 40ms' — that row has no verb frame so the proposed regex leaves it alone; and 'capped at 60s server-side' likewise. I traced all three `passes` rows against the proposed pattern and none matches. `it('no comment or test name quotes a measurement')` WILL fail until the four offending comments are rewritten — that failure is the point, but it must be landed in the same change or the suite goes red.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the matcher is widened and the four comments are not rewritten, the suite is red rather than silently under-grading — which is the correct direction. If the comments are rewritten and the matcher is not widened, the four instances are gone and the class is still ungraded, which is exactly how this rule reached its current state.

summary: seam.ts is THE PRODUCT and the only specification an out-of-tree plugin author reads, and it declares replayability for `FetchRecentResult.nextCursor` only ("The cursor to persist and replay verbatim as the next `since`"). `Message.cursor` is described merely as "Monotonic position of THIS message within its topic — the order key". But core hands a message's own cursor back to the agent as `nextCursor` on the truncation path, and the frozen conformance suite enforces the stronger rule. The two spellings are the same TypeScript brand, so nothing at compile time or in seam.ts's prose tells an author that a paging-token `nextCursor` distinct from message cursors is non-conformant — and message.ts's own BuildMessageInput doc actively invites that split ("`backendMsgId` and `cursor` are not always the same value").
failure: A plugin whose `nextCursor` is an opaque paging token (a Matrix `/messages` `end` token, a Discord `before` handle) while `Message.cursor` is a per-message ordinal satisfies seam.ts as written. Call `parley_fetch_recent({ topic: 'ctx', limit: 5 })` against a page the backend returns with 12 own-topic messages: transport/tools.ts:162 takes the `kept.length < own.length` branch and returns `nextCursor = kept.at(-1)!.cursor` — a message ordinal, not a paging token. The agent replays it as `since` and the backend either rejects it or resumes from an unrelated position, silently skipping or replaying the remaining 7 messages. packages/conformance/src/cases/concurrency.ts:98 (`fetchRecent({ topic: t, since: all[k]!.cursor })`) is the only place the requirement exists.
remediation: State the rule in seam.ts where the type is defined: on `Message.cursor`, add that it MUST be accepted verbatim as `FetchRecentArgs.since` and yield exactly the messages after it — i.e. the cursor space of `Message.cursor` and of `nextCursor` is one space — and mirror it in the numbered conformance contract at the top of the file and in the README's "A conforming backend guarantees" list (which today lists only two guarantees). Optionally add a third clause to that list so the doc and packages/conformance agree on the count.
testUpgrade: Add a clause-coverage assertion to packages/conformance/src/clauses.ts style: derive the numbered guarantees from seam.ts's own doc block and require one suite case per clause, so a rule the suite enforces but the seam does not state (or vice versa) fails as an unmatched clause. Then parameterise the since-replay case over cursor SOURCE — {nextCursor from a page, cursor of the last message on a page, cursor of a mid-page message} x {cold topic, resumed topic, concurrently-written topic} — so the requirement is graded from every place core actually obtains a cursor rather than only from the middle-of-a-concurrent-topic instance.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing executable — this is a doc/contract change to seam.ts plus a README bullet. It relies on packages/conformance/src/cases/concurrency.ts:98 continuing to enforce the rule for shipped backends, which I read and confirmed.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at runtime; it newly makes a paging-token-only plugin visibly non-conformant to a reader instead of only to the suite.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I checked packages/bridge-core/src/index.test.ts's JSDoc-link scanner (it only faults `{@link}`/backtick references to symbols the barrel withholds — the added prose names `since` and `Message.cursor`, both exported) and readme-truth.test.ts (its CEILING_CLAIM scan and config-sample execution are untouched by a seam prose change). The README's "guarantees two things" sentence would need the count updated if a third clause is added.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Documenting it does not stop a non-conformant plugin from shipping; only the conformance suite does that, and it already runs for in-repo backends. What stays broken is an out-of-tree plugin that never runs the suite — for which the doc is the only defence, which is precisely why the doc is the fix here rather than a code change.

summary: `let config = env['PARLEY_CONFIG'] ?? 'parley.config.yaml';` uses `??`, which only fires on null/undefined, so an exported-but-empty `PARLEY_CONFIG` becomes the literal empty path. This is the same shape the module's own doc calls out and the same shape the very next branch refuses explicitly: `--config=` with an empty value returns `{ kind: 'error', message: '--config= requires a path' }`. The two spellings of "a config path whose value the shell ate" are handled inconsistently — one is a located parse error naming the offender, the other is a filesystem error from a different layer.
failure: `PARLEY_CONFIG= parley-sqlite` (a systemd unit or wrapper script that exports the variable unconditionally) -> parseArgs returns `{ kind: 'run', config: '' }` -> `loadConfig('')` -> `parley-sqlite: fatal: Error: cannot read config : ENOENT: no such file or directory, open ''`. The diagnostic names neither PARLEY_CONFIG nor the default, and the argv parser — the layer whose whole documented job is to refuse an argument it cannot honour before any transport exists — reported success.
remediation: Read the variable through a guard rather than `??`: `const fromEnv = env['PARLEY_CONFIG']; if (fromEnv === '') return { kind: 'error', message: 'PARLEY_CONFIG is set but empty; unset it to use parley.config.yaml, or give it a path' }; let config = fromEnv ?? 'parley.config.yaml';`. Refusing rather than falling back keeps the module's stated rule (never silently start the default deployment) true for both spellings.
testUpgrade: Parameterise the CLI's config-source table over SOURCE x VALUE: source in {argv `--config <v>`, argv `--config=<v>`, env PARLEY_CONFIG}, value in {a path, '', ' ', a value starting with `-`, absent}, with the expected ParsedArgs derived once per value class rather than per source — so any source that answers a degenerate value differently from its siblings is a red cell. The existing `it('PARLEY_CONFIG supplies the default and an explicit --config beats it')` covers only the happy path and cannot see this.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: parseArgs's existing `{ kind: 'error' }` arm and runBackendCli's handling of it at backend-cli.ts:130-133 (`process.stderr.write(...); process.exit(2)`), which I read — an error kind exits 2 before any transport is built, which is the behaviour wanted here.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `PARLEY_CONFIG=''` with no `--config` on argv — today a run against the empty path, after the fix an exit-2 with a named cause. Note it must be checked BEFORE the argv loop assigns `config`, or an explicit `--config a.yaml` alongside an empty PARLEY_CONFIG would be refused when it should win.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. `it('PARLEY_CONFIG supplies the default and an explicit --config beats it')` in src/cli/backend-cli.test.ts passes `{ PARLEY_CONFIG: 'env.yaml' }` and `{}` via OPTS.env, never ''; the REFUSED/HONOURED tables are argv-only and use `env: {}`. I checked both tables row by row.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the guard is placed after the argv loop instead of before it, `--config good.yaml` under an empty PARLEY_CONFIG is refused — turning a confusing error into a broken working invocation. The ordering is the whole fix.

summary: `MIN_HASH_LEN = 10` (40 bits) is exactly the width DEFAULT_HASH_LEN's own JSDoc records as demonstrably insufficient: "That is why 40 bits was not enough: over the Matrix alias fold, which rejects everything outside [A-Za-z0-9._-], three lossy positions in a victim topic already put a collision in reach, and a collision routes one topic's traffic into another's backend channel." The RangeError guarding the floor says "A shorter suffix is brute-forceable, and two topics sharing one backend name cross-deliver" — a sentence equally true at 10. safeName is barrel-exported public API, so an out-of-tree plugin author reading MIN_HASH_LEN's doc ("A caller may ask for this narrow a suffix deliberately") is told the floor is a legitimate deliberate choice by the same module that records it as the failure it was raised from.
failure: `safeName(topic, matrixAliasFold, { hashLen: MIN_HASH_LEN })` mints a 10-hex (40-bit) suffix and returns normally. Against the Matrix alias fold, an attacker who can create topics searches raw strings sharing the victim's sanitized form; with three lossy positions the fold-side search space is small and the digest side is 2^40, which the same file's own doc says puts a collision in reach — and a collision routes one topic's traffic into another's room. Nothing in the API or the error text warns the caller.
remediation: Either raise MIN_HASH_LEN to the width the rationale supports (16, i.e. make DEFAULT the floor and delete the separate constant), or keep the floor and change its doc + the RangeError text to state what an operator is buying at each width — replacing "A caller may ask for this narrow a suffix deliberately" with the cost, e.g. "below 16 the suffix is 2^(4*hashLen) and the Matrix alias fold puts a chosen-name collision in reach at 10". Raising it is the safer of the two: `git grep 'hashLen'` shows no shipped backend passes the option, so the only breakage is a hypothetical external caller.
testUpgrade: Turn the hash-width rows in stated-bounds.test.ts into a table keyed on SECURITY RATIONALE rather than on the constants: one row per width in {MIN_HASH_LEN, DEFAULT_HASH_LEN, MAX_HASH_LEN} asserting both the minted width AND that the module's own prose for that width does not contradict the prose for another (e.g. no width is simultaneously described as mintable and as 'not enough'). A parameterised doc-vs-constant consistency case catches the class — a floor, a default and a ceiling drifting apart — rather than this one pair.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: topic-name.ts's `if (!Number.isInteger(hashLen) || hashLen < MIN_HASH_LEN || hashLen > MAX_HASH_LEN)` guard, and stated-bounds.test.ts's BOUNDS row 'safeName hash suffix floor (MIN_HASH_LEN)' whose probe derives every value from the constant (inside = bound+1, outside = bound-1) and so follows a raised floor automatically.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: if MIN_HASH_LEN is raised to 16: `safeName(t, fold, { hashLen: 10 })` through `{ hashLen: 15 }`, all accepted today. No in-repo caller passes hashLen at all (verified by grep), so nothing shipped changes behaviour.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: raising the floor breaks `it.each([MIN_HASH_LEN, MIN_HASH_LEN + 1, 20, MAX_HASH_LEN])('accepts hashLen %s')` only in the sense that its first two rows move with the constant (they are derived, so they follow); it DOES break the literal row `it.each([0, 1, 2, 4, 8, -4, 2.5, NaN, Infinity])('rejects hashLen %s')` not at all, and it breaks stated-bounds.test.ts's CAPACITIES pin `{ name: 'MIN_HASH_LEN', expected: 10 }` and its realistic-input probe, both of which must be updated to the new literal. Those two are the named breakages. The doc-only variant of the fix breaks nothing.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Changing only the prose leaves a 40-bit width mintable through public API; changing only the constant leaves DEFAULT_HASH_LEN's paragraph explaining why 40 bits failed with no constant it refers to, which is a fresh doc rot. Both halves belong in one change.

summary: The long-poll reader cap's RELEASE is graded by nothing. Deleting `this.blockingReaders--` from blockingRead's `finally` leaves all 980 tests in the package green, while permanently disabling native long-polling after the eighth blocking fetchRecent in a process. Every cap row in live-connections.test.ts uses a fresh plugin per row and measures only concurrent fan-out, so the counter never has to come back down; conformance's `native-block-actually-waits` clause — which exists for exactly this failure — is asserted once per plugin instance.
failure: Mutant applied (delete `this.blockingReaders--;`), full suite run against a live Redis: 980 passed / 0 failed. A probe issuing ten sequential `fetchRecent({topic, since, blockMs: 400})` on one plugin measured [430,501,501,502,502,503,502,504,1,0] ms — calls 9 and 10 return instantly with an empty page, so core's fetchRecentBlocking degrades to a `block_poll_interval_ms` poll against the backend for the rest of the process, which is the hot loop clauses.ts names.
remediation: Add a repetition axis to the long-poll coverage rather than another single-shot row: on ONE connected plugin, run `MAX_BLOCKING_READERS + 2` blocking fetchRecents SEQUENTIALLY at a cursor sitting at the tail, and assert every one of them spends at least its granted budget (and that `proxy.accepted()` grew by one reader per call). No src change is required — the decrement is present and correct.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a bounded resource whose acquire is graded and whose release is not'. In packages/bridge-redis/test/live-connections.test.ts, parameterize the existing cap block over a DISPOSITION axis {concurrent, sequential} crossed with a count derived from `MAX_BLOCKING_READERS` (n = 1, MAX, MAX+2, 2*MAX), asserting for the sequential rows that elapsed >= blockMs for EVERY call and that readers opened == n. Widen the same way in packages/conformance/src/cases/blocking.ts: repeat the `native-block-actually-waits` assertion k times on the same plugin with k taken from the context (default 3) so any backend holding a pooled/counted resource per blocking fetch is graded on giving it back. The existing rows too narrow to catch this are live-connections.test.ts 'a blocking fetch opens a bounded number of readers' (one fresh plugin per row) and blocking.ts arm (b).

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing in src. The test relies on `MAX_BLOCKING_READERS` already being exported from packages/bridge-redis/src/index.ts:45 and on `withProxiedPlugin`/`peakLive` in live-connections.test.ts, plus the branch `if (this.blockingReaders >= MAX_BLOCKING_READERS) return [];` (index.ts:236) staying the only early-return before `newReader()`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none (test-only)
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I re-ran the full package suite unmutated (980 green) and the proposed rows only add assertions; the sequential row costs ~MAX*blockMs of wall clock, so keep blockMs small (200ms) or it pushes past the 20s testTimeout in vitest.config.ts.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing stays broken: the decrement is present today, so this closes a coverage hole rather than a live defect. If it is NOT applied, the next refactor of blockingRead's finally (e.g. moving retireReader out of it) can drop the decrement with the suite green.

summary: `entryTimestamp` clamps any negative millisecond to 0, silently rewriting every pre-1970 timestamp to the epoch. The clamp exists (per its own comment) to keep a `RangeError` out of the seam when a foreign writer chooses an entry-id millisecond past what `Date` can represent — but `Date` represents -8,640,000,000,000,000 through +8,640,000,000,000,000, so the lower bound is off by the whole negative half of the range. The live-stream `from-ts` spelling table has no pre-epoch row, so nothing sees it.
failure: `XADD <key> * sender a content hi ts 1960-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` from an independent client, then `plugin.fetchRecent({topic})` -> `Message.timestamp === '1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'` (reproduced against a live Redis). Expected '1960-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'.
remediation: In packages/bridge-redis/src/entry.ts, change the guard to `ms >= -MAX_DATE_MS && ms <= MAX_DATE_MS ? ms : 0` and reword MAX_DATE_MS's comment to name both ends of Date's range.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a range clamp asserted only at the end it was written for'. In packages/bridge-redis/test/live-stream.test.ts, derive the `from-ts` spelling rows from Date's own bounds instead of hand-picking modern dates: add rows for `new Date(-LAST_DATE_MS).toISOString()`, `1960-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`, `1969-12-31T23:59:59.999Z`, `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` and `new Date(LAST_DATE_MS).toISOString()`, each declaring the instant it must DERIVE (not merely that it parses). Cross them with the existing fetchRecent/subscribe path axis so neither half can be fixed alone.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `MAX_DATE_MS = 8_640_000_000_000_000` (entry.ts:12) and `new Date(ms).toISOString()`; the id path still cannot produce a negative ms because `Number('<digits>')` is non-negative, so only the `Date.parse(ts)` branch changes behaviour.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `ts: '1960-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'` now yields '1960-01-01T00:00:00.000Z' instead of the epoch; `ts: new Date(-8.64e15).toISOString()` yields the expanded-year ISO form '-271821-04-20T00:00:00.000Z'.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — nothing that is accepted today becomes an error.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I read every timestamp assertion in packages/bridge-redis/test/live-stream.test.ts: `foreignEntries` from-ts rows are all >= 2020, `idRows` uses WELL_KNOWN_TS (2020) or derives from a non-negative uint64 id, and 'normalizes a foreign entry arriving over the LIVE path too' uses '12/25/2021'. The conformance suite asserts parseability, not a specific instant. No row asserts the epoch for a negative ms.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while something downstream assumes a 4-digit year, an expanded-year ISO string ('-271821-04-20T...') now reaches Message.timestamp; DESIGN §5 says ISO 8601 and informational-only, and the suite's own round-trip check `toBe(new Date(Date.parse(t)).toISOString())` still holds, but a strict YYYY-MM-DD consumer would see a shape it has never seen. Clamping to `-MAX_DATE_MS` rather than to 0 is the whole of the fix; nothing else stays broken.

summary: The 'a server-gated file has no ungated cases' rule is justified by a claim about CI that is false, and cannot see the one file in this package that most needs it. Its comment states 'CI's skip gate fails only files where EVERY assertion skipped' — but scripts/assert-no-skipped-tests.mjs judges each `describe` GROUP (its own docstring says so explicitly, and names the per-file rule as the one it replaced). So the hazard the rule exists for no longer exists. Meanwhile `GATED_BLOCK = /describe\.skipIf\(/` does not match conformance.test.ts, which gates itself with `if (await isRedisUp(REDIS_URL))` + `describe.skip`, so the rule silently exempts it. And the rule prescribes a file layout ('move the ungated blocks into a file of their own'), which CLAUDE.md's standing rule on architectural tests forbids a ratchet from driving.
failure: Appended `describe('MUTANT ungated block in a server-gated file', () => { it('runs unconditionally', () => { expect(1).toBe(1); }); });` to packages/bridge-redis/test/conformance.test.ts and ran test-hygiene.test.ts: 41/41 passed. The exact shape the rule bans is invisible in the file the rule most needs to cover.
remediation: Two independent edits. (1) Correct or delete the premise: the comment at test-hygiene.test.ts:71-75 describes a per-FILE gate that scripts/assert-no-skipped-tests.mjs no longer implements. (2) Decide the rule on its merits given the per-group gate — I would delete the whole second `describe` block, because the CI gate already fails a run in which any describe group ran nothing, which is the property the rule was proxying for, and the rule additionally cements file layout. If it is kept instead, derive `gated` from 'the file skips itself when the server is away' rather than from one spelling of the gate — e.g. flag any file that references `isRedisUp` AND contains a top-level `describe(` — so conformance.test.ts stops being exempt.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a lint whose subject set is derived from one spelling of the thing it audits'. Wherever this rule survives, add an inverse arm that is generated rather than sampled: enumerate every file in test/ that imports `isRedisUp` from support.ts, and assert that set is exactly the set the rule classified as gated — so a file that gates itself by a mechanism the regex does not know fails HERE rather than escaping. Pair it with a row asserting scripts/assert-no-skipped-tests.mjs's granularity directly (feed it a synthetic report with one skipped group beside a passing group and expect exit 1), so the rule's stated justification is graded instead of asserted in prose.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: scripts/assert-no-skipped-tests.mjs `removedCoverage`, specifically `groupOf(file, assertion) = [file.name, ...ancestorTitles].join(' > ')` and `.filter(([, seen]) => seen.ran === 0 && seen.skipped.length > 0)` — that is the branch that makes conformance.test.ts's `describe.skip('seam conformance: redis (no server at ...)')` group fail CI on its own.

summary: `deliver` absorbs both a throw and a rejection from the handler and writes nothing, ever. The loop is scrupulous about the other half of the same hazard — a server fault that keeps failing gets DEGRADED after 5 consecutive failures precisely 'so that a fault the loop keeps RETRYING does not look identical to a quiet topic' — but a handler that fails on every message produces the identical end state (subscribe() resolved, core still advertising the topic as subscribed, live push delivering nothing) with zero lines. The absorbing is right; the silence is the defect, and `deliver`'s own comment invokes 'silently, since catch-up keeps working and nothing writes a line' as the harm it is preventing.
failure: `subscribe(t, () => { throw new Error('handler blew up'); })`, then post 100 messages: every message is dropped from the live path, `disconnect()` reports nothing, stderr is empty, and the operator's only signal is that the `<channel>` events stopped. Compare an XREAD failing 5 times in a row, which writes 'parley-redis: live delivery DEGRADED for topic ...'.
remediation: In read-loop.ts, count consecutive handler failures per loop and write one line — mirroring reportLiveDeliveryDegraded's wording and its once-only discipline — after the same DEGRADED_AFTER_FAILURES threshold, resetting on the first success. Add the reporter to diagnostics.ts beside the existing three so the topic goes through `fromCaller` and nothing of the handler's own error text is emitted unsanitised.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'one delivery path, two failure sources, only one of them diagnosed'. In packages/bridge-redis/test/live-connections.test.ts, parameterize the existing 'a misbehaving handler never disables live push' block over a SOURCE axis {server refusal, handler throw, handler rejection} crossed with a DURATION axis {clears after 3, never clears}, asserting the same invariant for every cell: a fault that never clears produces exactly one stderr line naming the topic, and a fault that clears produces none. Today's rows fix SOURCE at 'handler' and assert only that later messages are still offered, so the diagnostic half is structurally unreachable.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `deliver` (read-loop.ts:31) — specifically that the rejection arm is `void Promise.resolve(handler(message)).catch(...)`, so a failure is observable only inside that catch and inside the surrounding try; the counter must be threaded from runReadLoop into deliver, which currently takes only (handler, message).
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — no input starts being refused; only a line is added.

remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied and the underlying absorbing were wrong, the line would announce a topic whose live push is dead without ending the loop — which is the intended behaviour, not a mask. If NOT applied, a handler that fails on every message is indistinguishable from a quiet topic, which is the exact condition the STOPPED and DEGRADED lines exist to make distinguishable.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The new counter lives in runReadLoop's own closure, one per subscribed topic, and is only touched from that loop's single-threaded continuation chain; deliver dispatches synchronously, so two handler failures for the same topic cannot interleave. Two callers = two subscribes = two loops = two counters, no shared state.

summary: `assertMintedCursor` runs `BigInt(part)` over caller-controlled text before deciding to reject it. `since` reaches the plugin as a bare `z.string()` with no max length (packages/bridge-core/src/transport/tools.ts:93), so an MCP client — the model, or a remote chat peer in the OAuth deployment — chooses the length. Every other caller-text path in this plugin is bounded (`fromCaller` -> `sanitizeBody`), but here the bound is applied only to the error message that is composed AFTER the work. The event loop it blocks is the one serving every subscribed topic's read loop and the JSON-RPC transport.
failure: `plugin.fetchRecent({ topic, since: asCursor('9'.repeat(5_000_000)) })` blocks for 447 ms before rejecting with 'parley-redis: malformed cursor ...' (measured through the real plugin). Raw BigInt cost measured at 71 ms for 1e6 digits and 1018 ms for 1e7. During that window no subscribed topic delivers and no MCP request is served.
remediation: Reject on length before touching BigInt: in assertMintedCursor, fail fast when `since.length` exceeds a generous ceiling, then run the existing pattern and range checks. Do NOT set the ceiling at the canonical 41 characters — see newlyRejects.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'caller-controlled text doing unbounded work before the guard that bounds it'. Add a generated row set to packages/bridge-redis/test/hostile-server.test.ts's caller-channel table: for each channel already listed there (cursor, topic, each rejected backend_config knob), feed payloads at 1e3, 1e5 and 1e7 characters and assert BOTH the existing safety invariants AND that the call settles within a fixed wall-clock budget (say 100 ms) — a timing bound, so it is a property of the guard's cost rather than of its output. The existing rows already pad to `MAX_ERROR_BODY * 20` but assert only length-invariance of the message, never elapsed time, which is why this is invisible today.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `CURSOR_PATTERN = /^\d+(-\d+)?$/` and `MAX_ID_COMPONENT = 2n**64n - 1n` (entry-id.ts:6,8); the new check must run BEFORE the `.every(part => BigInt(part) <= MAX_ID_COMPONENT)` in the same expression, and must throw through the same `pluginError` so `labelled()` still recognises it as this plugin's own (index.ts:102).
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A cursor longer than the ceiling. THE TRAP: the canonical maximum is 41 characters (20 + '-' + 20), but packages/bridge-redis/test/live-stream.test.ts deliberately requires zero-padded spellings to be honoured — `respell(id, 3, 3)` on the ceiling id produces a 47-character cursor, and the 'spellings' axis exists precisely so a guard cannot compare cursors by string. A 41-character cap would redden the ceiling x spelling rows in 'a cursor past the high-water mark self-heals' and 'echoes a cursor at or below the tail'. Use a generous cap (>= 1024) or strip leading zeros before BigInt.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: With a generous cap: none found — I checked live-stream.test.ts's `spellings`/`shapes`/`belowTailShapes` (longest generated cursor 47 chars), hostile-server.test.ts's cursor channel (payload + MAX_ERROR_BODY*20 of padding, which is meant to be REJECTED and still would be, just faster), and core-catchup.test.ts's foreign cursors (all short). With a 41-char cap: eight rows in live-stream.test.ts fail.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: The bug is the unbounded work, not the rejection — the cursor is already correctly refused, just expensively. If the cap is applied, nothing else stays broken. If it is applied at 41 characters, it trades a latency defect for a correctness regression in the self-heal, which is strictly worse.

It is not a cost; it is optional.

Add one audit that globs `packages/bridge-core/src/**/*.ts` (excluding `*.test.ts`), finds every `new RegExp(` occurrence, and requires each to appear in a registry keyed by an anchor the scan itself produces — failing on an unregistered hit rather than pinning a count. summary: `defaultReadStatePath` uses `process.env.XDG_STATE_HOME ?? join(homedir(), '.local', 'state')`. `??` only falls back on `undefined`, so an XDG_STATE_HOME set to the empty string is taken as the base directory. `path.join('', 'parley', id, 'read-state.json')` collapses to a RELATIVE path, and `ReadStateStore`'s only path guard is `filePath.length === 0`, so it is adopted silently. The XDG Base Directory spec says an empty value must be treated as unset, and this function's own JSDoc writes the shell form `${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}`, whose `:-` means exactly 'unset OR empty'. The sibling test at read-state.test.ts:356 reasons about this identical hazard for `state_path` and guards it there; the env path was left unguarded.
failure: With `XDG_STATE_HOME=''` (which some login shells and container entrypoints export) and `instance_id: ctx-payments`: `defaultReadStatePath('ctx-payments')` returns `"parley/ctx-payments/read-state.json"` (reproduced with node). buildBridge then creates `./parley/ctx-payments/` under whatever CWD the agent was launched in — a git worktree, a repo the user is editing — and the read cursor is now CWD-keyed. Launch the same bridge from a different directory and `readState.get(topic)` returns undefined, so catch-up cold-starts, re-drains the recent window and rewrites the state file in the new directory, forever.
remediation: Fall back on empty as well as undefined: `const raw = process.env.XDG_STATE_HOME; const base = raw !== undefined && raw.length > 0 ? raw : join(homedir(), '.local', 'state');`. Do not additionally reject a relative XDG_STATE_HOME here — that is the operator's own setting and rejecting it would break deployments that work today.
testUpgrade: This is the class 'an optional string read with `??` treats "" as configured'. Table every optional string core reads from env or config that becomes a filesystem path, and assert for each that unset and empty produce the SAME absolute path: `[['XDG_STATE_HOME', () => defaultReadStatePath('i')], ...]` × `[undefined, '', '   ']`, asserting `isAbsolute(p)` and equality between the unset and empty rows. The existing `it('default path is namespaced by instanceId')` sets XDG_STATE_HOME to a real mkdtemp dir and could never have seen this; the existing `it('refuses an empty path instead of adopting it')` grades `state_path`, the sibling that WAS fixed.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `homedir()` from node:os and `join` from node:path — both already imported here. Nothing else.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: nothing new is accepted; an empty XDG_STATE_HOME now resolves to the documented ~/.local/state default instead of a relative path
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. read-state.test.ts lines 112-123 and 192 set XDG_STATE_HOME to a non-empty mkdtemp directory, and lines 114-115 restore it; the delete-when-undefined branch exercises the fallback, which this change preserves. `packages/bridge-telegram/test/docs.test.ts:545` runs the same set/unset pair for the telegram store path — a different function, untouched.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: The identical `??`-on-XDG_STATE_HOME bug exists at packages/bridge-telegram/src/config.ts:119 and is NOT fixed by this change; the telegram observed-message store lands relative to CWD under the same condition, which is worse there because losing that file invalidates every cursor it minted. That belongs to the telegram package, so I am reporting it here rather than fixing it across the seam.

summary: In `createRemoteHttpApp().listen`, `announce()` runs inside the `app.listen` 'listening' callback, between `s.off('error', failed)` and `resolve(s)`, with no try/catch. `startPresenceLoop` throws a RangeError for a `presence.heartbeat_ms` outside [1, MAX_TIMER_MS]. The throw escapes an EventEmitter handler as an uncaughtException, `resolve` is never reached, and because `binding = bound.catch(...)` is derived from that same never-settling promise, `close()`'s first line `await binding` hangs forever too. The stdio root does the equivalent call inside `attach`'s try/catch with a full `releaseAll()` rollback; the HTTP root does not.
failure: Reproduced. `createRemoteHttpApp(plugin, { ...parseConfig(...), presence: { enabled: true, heartbeat_ms: 2**31 } }, { insecureNoAuth: true }).listen(0)` — probe output: `LISTEN OUTCOME: NEVER SETTLED | uncaught: presence heartbeatMs must be in [1, 2147483647] (got 2147483648)` after a 1.5 s race fence. The socket is bound and `httpServer` is assigned, but the caller's `await listen()` never returns and the `finally { await close() }` that a composition root would run also never returns. `createRemoteHttpApp` takes a `ParleyConfig` TYPE, not a zod-parsed value, so an embedder that builds the object literally (as core's own tests do) reaches this.
remediation: Wrap the callback body so every way it can fail lowers the latch, exactly as the surrounding `try`/`catch (err) { failed(err as Error); }` already does for the synchronous bind: `const s = app.listen(port, host, (err?: Error) => { if (err) { failed(err); return; } s.off('error', failed); try { announce(); } catch (e) { failed(e as Error); return; } resolve(s); });`. `httpServer = s` has already been assigned by the time the 'listening' event fires, so a caller that catches the rejection and calls `close()` still finds and closes the bound socket. Complementarily, validate `cfg.presence.heartbeat_ms` with `isArmableDelay` at construction time, so a bad cadence fails before a socket exists rather than after.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a step inside a promise-settling callback can throw, and the promise is then never settled'. Parameterize over every step `listen`'s callback performs, injected with each shape from the existing `src/testing/failure-shapes.ts` (sync throw, async reject, never-settles), asserting for each cell BOTH that `listen()` settles within a budget (rejecting, not hanging) AND that a subsequent `close()` settles within its budget. `root-teardown-bounds.test.ts`'s 'remote HTTP close() is bounded whatever the presence post does' table only varies what `post` does AFTER the loop starts — it never makes `startPresenceLoop` itself throw, which is why it is green today.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `failed(err)` at http.ts:274, which sets `starting = false` and rejects — so the server stays retryable. And on `httpServer = s` (line 293) executing before the 'listening' callback fires: `app.listen` returns synchronously and the event is emitted on a later tick, which I verified by the probe reaching the callback at all.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `listen()` now REJECTS (instead of hanging) when presence cannot be started; the complementary construction-time check additionally rejects `createRemoteHttpApp` with an out-of-range `presence.heartbeat_ms`, which today builds an app successfully
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I grepped every `createRemoteHttpApp` call site in the target's tests (http-request-path, http-gating, root-teardown-bounds, front-doors, testing/http-app.ts) — all derive cfg from `parseConfig`, which zod-bounds heartbeat_ms to [1, MAX_TIMER_MS], so `announce()` cannot throw in any of them and the new try/catch is inert there. `degenerate-bounds.test.ts`'s KNOBS table covers `startPresenceLoop` directly, not through `createRemoteHttpApp`.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: The try/catch fixes the class (any throw in the callback now rejects rather than strands). The construction-time validation alone would NOT: it closes only the one known thrower and leaves the strand-on-throw shape in place for the next step added to that callback, so applying only the narrow half hides this instance while the class stays open. Neither half addresses that `close()` unconditionally awaits `binding` with no timeout — a bind that hangs (not throws) still wedges teardown, and that remains broken after this fix.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The orderings that matter: (a) listen() → announce throws → failed() rejects → caller's catch calls close(); close() awaits `binding`, which is now the settled `bound.catch(() => undefined)`, then closes the bound socket — terminates. (b) close() called concurrently while listen() is still mid-bind: close awaits `binding`, which now always settles, so close proceeds; `starting` is still true across close's awaits so a third caller's listen() rejects rather than racing. (c) Two callers both invoking listen(): the synchronous `starting` latch at line 269 admits exactly one; the loser rejects before touching the callback, so the new catch cannot be entered twice for one socket.

summary: `BlockingFetchOptions.now` is documented as 'Monotonic clock in ms. Default `Date.now`.' `Date.now` is a wall clock and is not monotonic. `fetchRecentBlocking` computes `deadline = now() + blockMs` once and then compares `now() >= deadline` on every iteration, so a backward wall-clock step extends the long poll by the size of the step. The same file's sibling `engine/presence-reach.ts` already uses `performance.now()` where it needs a real meter, so core knows the distinction and states it wrongly here.
failure: A `parley_fetch_recent` with `block_ms: 60000` starts at wall time T. Ten seconds in, NTP steps the clock back one hour. `deadline` is still T+60000 while `now()` returns T-3590000, so `now() >= deadline` stays false for the next ~60 minutes: the loop keeps issuing `plugin.fetchRecent` every `blockPollIntervalMs`, holding one HTTP connection and one MCP tool call for an hour instead of a minute. The client-side tool timeout fires long before, but the server keeps polling until `extra.signal` aborts — and on stdio there is no socket teardown to force it.
remediation: Default `now` to `performance.now()` and document it as monotonic (matching `DEFAULT_REACH_BUDGET.now` in presence-reach.ts), or, if `Date.now` must stay for injectability reasons, change the JSDoc to say 'wall clock' and clamp the per-iteration remaining budget so a backward step cannot extend the deadline: `deadline = Math.min(deadline, now() + opts.blockMs)`.
testUpgrade: This is the class 'a deadline computed from a clock that can move backwards'. Table every deadline/budget in engine/ and transport/ against an injected clock that steps BACKWARD mid-operation (`fetchRecentBlocking`'s `now`, `presence-reach`'s `ReachBudget.now`, and any later one), asserting each still terminates within its nominal budget measured on a separate monotonic reference. The existing blocking-fetch cases 'returns an empty page with a stable cursor at the deadline' and the abort table all use monotonically increasing injected clocks, so none can see a step back.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `performance.now()` being available on Node >=22 (package.json engines) — presence-reach.ts already calls it unguarded, so this adds no new platform assumption. It also relies on every existing caller passing `now` only as an override: tools.ts:124 passes `deps.now`, which `toolDepsFor` leaves undefined in production.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — this changes only which clock the default deadline is measured on
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Possibly `blocking-fetch.test.ts`'s cases that pass an injected `now` returning Date-scale values while also relying on the DEFAULT sleep, if any mix the two; I did not enumerate them line by line. The `min(deadline, now()+blockMs)` variant is safe against that because it never changes the clock, only clamps forward drift — I would take that variant if the injected-clock cases redden.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied and the wall clock is still used elsewhere for a duration (I found none in the target), those remain wrong. Fixing only the JSDoc and not the code leaves the hour-long hold in place — the doc change alone is the hiding option, so both halves have to land.

summary: `beat()` wraps the whole encode+post in `try { ... } catch { }` with no log, ever. The comment justifies it as 'Best-effort: a dropped beat is harmless; TTL reconciles'. That reasoning holds for a transient hiccup and fails completely for a permanent one: a beat rejected every time (content over the backend's message-size limit, presence topic not writable by this credential, revoked token, a plugin that always throws) means this bridge never appears in ANY peer's `parley_list_users` for the process lifetime, with zero output on any channel. CLAUDE.md names fail-fast / no silent no-ops as a design principle, and the sibling `startPushLoop` already ships the right shape: warn once per loop.
failure: A bridge configured with 64 topics of up to MAX_TOPIC_LEN each produces a beat body of tens of kilobytes. On a backend whose per-message limit is smaller (Telegram 4096 bytes, Zulip 10000), `plugin.post(presenceTopic, ...)` rejects on every hello and every heartbeat. Observable result: the operator sees a healthy bridge serving tools normally, every peer's `parley_list_users` returns a roster that does not contain it, `truncated` is false so the answer reads as complete, and there is no log line anywhere to explain it.
remediation: Adopt the warn-once shape `startPushLoop` uses: hoist a `let warned = false` into `startPresenceLoop` and, in the catch, emit `console.error('[parley] presence beat failed; this bridge will not appear in any peer roster: ...')` the first time, then stay quiet. Do not log per beat — the heartbeat is on an interval and a per-beat log is its own denial of service against the operator's log. Keep the failure swallowed; only the silence is the defect.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a fire-and-forget seam call whose permanent failure is indistinguishable from success'. `unhandled-rejection.test.ts` already derives the inventory of every fire-and-forget statement in engine/ + transport/ and tables it against `testing/failure-shapes.ts` for ABSORPTION; extend that same derived table with a second assertion per cell — that a failing call produces at least one `console.error` on its first occurrence and at most one across N repeats. That covers presence beats, push emits, and the response-close teardowns in one parameterized pass, and any later fire-and-forget site joins it automatically because the inventory is derived.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `console.error` as the existing diagnostic channel in this layer (catchup.ts:59, push-loop.ts:53, tools.ts:155 all use it), and on `warned` being per-loop rather than per-beat, mirroring push-loop.ts:48.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — behaviour is unchanged, only a diagnostic is added
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: `presence-loop.test.ts` and `unhandled-rejection.test.ts`'s 'presence %s whose post %s' rows drive failing posts through this catch. Neither asserts console silence as far as I read, but several tests in this package spy on console.error with `mockImplementation(() => {})` and some assert call counts (http-gating.test.ts:100 does). I did not run this change, so I cannot name a specific test that reddens — that is the check to run first.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is fixed by this in the failure itself: the bridge is still invisible in every roster, and a peer still cannot hand off to it. It converts an undiagnosable outcome into a diagnosable one. If the real goal is that presence not fail silently at all, the beat body should also be size-checked against a declared per-backend limit — which the seam does not expose, so that is a seam question, not a fix here.

summary: `startPushLoop`'s handler calls `seen.firstSeen(m.topic, m.backendMsgId)` BEFORE the mention filter, so with `live_push.mention_filter: true` every message that will be discarded still consumes a slot in the 4096-entry per-topic dedup window. The window's stated job (seen-set.ts:23) is 'to cover the overlap between a catch-up pull and the live poll'; spending it on messages that are never emitted shortens that overlap in proportion to how chatty the topic is. Swapping the two lines is behaviourally superior and, notably, leaves the entire suite green — I mutated it and got 3451 passed, byte-identical to baseline.
failure: mention_filter on, one busy topic, 5000 messages arrive of which the last mentions this agent. The first 4999 non-mentioning ids fill and roll the 4096-slot FIFO. Suppose the mentioning message was already pulled by `parley_fetch_recent` (which marked it seen) before the flood: its id has been evicted by messages that were never emitted, so when the plugin redelivers it across the catch-up/live boundary `firstSeen` answers true and the agent gets a duplicate `<channel>` event for a message it already read. With the filter first, those 4999 ids never enter the window and the pulled id survives.
remediation: Move the cheap, stateless filter ahead of the stateful one: `if (opts.mentionFilter && !m.mentions.includes(opts.identity)) return;` then `if (!seen.firstSeen(m.topic, m.backendMsgId)) return;`. The emitted set is identical either way; only the window's occupancy changes.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a bounded cache is charged for work that is subsequently discarded'. Parameterize over the push handler's filter stages: for each stage that DROPS a message (unsubscribed topic, mention filter), assert with a small injected `new SeenSet(n, m)` that a flood of dropped messages does not evict an id that was marked seen before the flood — i.e. `seen.has(topic, preloadedId)` stays true after N drops, for N >> n. The current `it('mention filter: only messages mentioning identity are pushed')` grades the emitted set, which is invariant under this bug, and the 'pull and push paths never deliver the same message twice' ORDERS table uses a default-capacity SeenSet and three messages, so neither can reach the eviction boundary.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `opts.mentionFilter` and `m.mentions` being pure reads with no side effect — they are (push-loop.ts:61 is a plain array membership test), so reordering cannot change what is emitted. And on the unsubscribed-topic check staying first, since it is the trust boundary and must run before anything touches `m`.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — the set of messages emitted as `<channel>` events is unchanged for every input
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — I applied exactly this swap and ran the full bridge-core suite: 3451 passed, 99 skipped, identical to the unmutated baseline. That green is simultaneously the proof the fix is safe and the evidence the class is untested.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: This does not fix the underlying fragility, which is that the dedup window's adequacy is entirely unmeasured — nothing anywhere asserts that the 4096/256 defaults actually cover a realistic catch-up/live overlap, so a different chatty-topic shape can still evict a legitimately-pulled id even with the filter reordered. It removes one avoidable consumer, not the risk.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The handler is invoked synchronously by the plugin, one message at a time, and both lines are synchronous — there is no await between them, so no interleaving is introduced. Two plugins calling the same handler concurrently is not possible on Node's single thread within one synchronous handler body.

summary: `emitterOf`'s JSDoc says 'Keep it DROPPED rather than truncated, exactly as `decodePresence` drops an over-long `handle`'. `decodePresence` does not drop an over-long handle — presence-beat.ts:142 returns `null` for the WHOLE record, and presence-beat.ts:139-140's own comment says so ('keep an over-long one REJECTING the record'). A reader of emitterOf would conclude that a beat whose self-reported `handle` exceeds MAX_HANDLE_LEN falls through to the `senderHandle` fallback on the next line. It never reaches emitterOf at all; the beat is gone, and that instance's liveness is lost entirely.
failure: Not a runtime failure — a documentation failure with a concrete wrong prediction. Input: a beat with `handle` of 129 characters and a valid `senderHandle` of 'alice'. The comment predicts the peer appears in the roster as 'alice' (fallback applied). Actual: `decodePresence` returns null at presence-beat.ts:142, `computeRoster` skips the message at line 157, and the peer does not appear at all. The two comments describe the same code and contradict each other.
remediation: Correct the sentence in emitterOf to describe what actually happens: the length cap here applies to the FALLBACK only, because an over-long self-reported `handle` has already cost the whole record at decode. Then keep the invariant it is really asserting — that neither path truncates — which is the part worth writing down.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'two caps on one identity field, applied at two sites with different dispositions'. Parameterize over `(handleLength, senderHandleLength) ∈ {under, exactly MAX_HANDLE_LEN, over}²` and assert the resulting roster entry (present-as-handle / present-as-sender / absent) for all nine cells, so the disposition of each site is pinned by behaviour rather than by prose. The existing HANDLE_CELLS rows in presence.test.ts:943 cover the over-long cases but do not cross them, so the interaction the comment describes is never exercised.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: presence-beat.ts:142 `if (handle !== undefined && handle.length > MAX_HANDLE_LEN) return null;` — the branch the comment misdescribes. Nothing else.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — this is a comment edit. The nine-cell test the testUpgrade proposes would pass against today's code; it exists to stop the two sites from drifting apart later.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is fixed. If the intended behaviour really is 'fall back to senderHandle when the self-reported handle is over-long', then the CODE is wrong at presence-beat.ts:142 and correcting the comment cements the wrong behaviour. I could not determine from DESIGN.md which disposition was intended, so I am reporting the contradiction rather than picking a side.

summary: `catchUpTopic`'s JSDoc describes two distinct behaviours — 'RESUMED (a cursor on disk): pages forward from that cursor until the topic is exhausted' vs 'COLD START (no cursor): reads the backend's most-recent `limit` window and adopts its tail' — as if `resumedFromDisk` selected between them. It does not: `resumedFromDisk` is used at line 54 solely to pick the `fetchWithResumeHint` error wrapper for page 0. Both cases run the identical paging loop, so a cold start also pages forward from the tail of that first window until an empty page.
failure: A reader (or an agent adding a backend) predicting behaviour from this doc gets it wrong for any plugin whose `since`-less read is not the most-recent window. Concretely: a plugin whose default window is the OLDEST `limit` messages (the seam text at seam.ts:52 says only 'the backend's default recent window', it does not forbid this) makes a cold start page through the entire topic history — up to MAX_CATCHUP_PAGES × limit round trips and that many read-state file rewrites — where the doc promises exactly one window read and a tail adoption.
remediation: State the one loop the code has: both cases page forward until an empty page or a cursor that does not advance; the difference is only the STARTING position (the stored cursor, or whatever the backend's default window ends at) and the resume-hint wrapping on page 0. Keep the genuinely load-bearing half of the current text — that anything older than a cold start's first window is outside this instance's horizon and is never drained.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'the doc claims a branch the code does not take'. Extend `catchup.test.ts`'s 'drained window depends on stored-cursor × page-size' table with a column asserting the NUMBER of `fetchRecent` calls per cell, for both the resumed and cold-start rows — the identical page-count arithmetic across the two is exactly what pins 'one loop, two starting positions' and would redden if someone later short-circuited the cold-start branch to match the prose.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: nothing — this is a comment edit against catchup.ts lines 51-75, whose only use of `resumedFromDisk` is the ternary at line 54.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none. The call-count assertions the testUpgrade adds pass against today's code; I did not write them, so treat that as untested.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is fixed. If the DESIGN intent really is that a cold start reads exactly one window and stops, then the CODE should return after page 0 when `!resumedFromDisk`, and rewriting the comment to match the code would cement a horizon wider than intended. DESIGN §7 does not settle it, so I am reporting the divergence rather than choosing.

summary: ParleyOAuthProvider.stop() clears six process-local Maps, but the only test that grades teardown (teardown.test.ts:181 'an access token minted before close does not survive it') hand-checks exactly one of them. The package already derives the store inventory twice — oauth-provider.test.ts:369 reads every `instanceof Map` off a live instance, and :604 scrapes `private readonly (\w+) = new Map` out of the source — and neither derivation is wired to the teardown assertion, so five of the six clears are uncovered.

Individually, dropping `this.refresh.clear()`, `this.pending.clear()`, `this.codes.clear()+this.redeeming.clear()` or `this.clients.clear()` each keeps the suite fully green. The defect that would ship behind that green: after `OAuthRemoteServer.close()` — whose JSDoc at remote.ts:40 says it 'drops every issued credential' — the provider still holds 30-day refresh tokens, live authorization codes, pending consents and DCR registrations, with the sweeper already cleared so nothing will ever evict them. A composition root that closes a front door and keeps the process alive (the multi-session example, a config reload, any test root) retains every credential for the life of the process.

Export or share the `PROVIDER_STORES`/`instanceof Map` derivation and add a parameterized case: for each derived store name, seed it through the public API (registerClient / authorize / completeConsent / exchangeAuthorizationCode / exchangeRefreshToken), call stop(), and assert `peek(p)[store].size === 0`. Keep the existing 'classifies every Map the provider actually keeps' row so a seventh store still fails to compile a row, and it now also fails the teardown row.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a lifecycle method that names N resources is graded on one of them'. Parameterize teardown over the SAME derived list the capacity suite uses (`Object.entries(provider).filter(([,v]) => v instanceof Map)`), one row per store, each with its own public-API seeder and an `expect(size).toBeGreaterThan(0)` pre-assertion so a row that seeded nothing cannot pass vacuously. Apply the same shape to createOAuthRemoteApp.close(): today teardown.test.ts:99 derives the interval set but the state set is hand-written; derive both. The existing too-narrow test is teardown.test.ts:181-199, which asserts only `peek.access.size === 0`.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: oauth-provider.test.ts:369-376 (`const maps = Object.entries(p).filter(([, v]) => v instanceof Map).map(([k]) => k)`) and the `peek()` internals cast already used throughout that file; teardown.test.ts's existing FACTORIES table for the close() half.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at runtime; it rejects any future stop()/close() that stops clearing a store the inventory derives
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — I ran the unmutated suite after adding a sixth store during a separate prototype and the only failures were the three inventory ratchets, which is the mechanism this upgrade hooks into
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken today; stop() is currently correct. Applied on its own it fixes no bug — it closes the hole that lets the bug ship silently. The residual risk if it is NOT applied is exactly the mutation above shipping unnoticed.

summary: exchangeRefreshToken rotates (revokeGrant + re-issue under the same grantId) but never detects reuse of a retired refresh token: `this.refresh.get(refreshToken)` simply misses and the call throws invalid_grant. OAuth 2.1 §4.3.1 / RFC 9700 §4.14.2 make replay detection the compensating control that makes non-sender-constrained rotating refresh tokens acceptable — on reuse the AS MUST revoke the whole grant. Parley leaves the attacker's freshly minted generation alive, so the legitimate client's failure is the only signal and nothing acts on it.
failure: 1) Owner consents -> grant G with refresh R1, access A1. 2) Attacker who has stolen R1 POSTs grant_type=refresh_token to /token: revokeGrant(G) kills R1/A1, issue(..., G) mints R2/A2 to the attacker. 3) The legitimate connector presents R1: `this.refresh.get(R1)` is undefined -> InvalidGrantError, and nothing else happens. The attacker keeps A2 (1h) and R2 (30d) and can rotate forever; the owner's only recovery is noticing the connector broke and re-entering the passphrase. remote.test.ts:382 'refresh_token rotation issues a new access token and one-time-uses the old refresh' asserts only `second.status >= 400`, so it pins the symptom and not the required grant revocation.
remediation: Keep a `retired: Map<string, RefreshRecord>` populated in revokeGrant alongside each `this.refresh.delete(k)`, swept on `expiresAtMs` by sweep() and cleared in stop(). At the top of exchangeRefreshToken, when the token is absent from `refresh` but present in `retired` and `retired.get(t).clientId === client.client_id`, call `revokeGrant(rec.grantId)` before throwing InvalidGrantError. Classify `retired` as owner-approved in clientStates() and name it in the class doc, and cap/sweep it so it is not a new unbounded store.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a rotated credential is refused but its successor survives'. Table-drive one row per credential family (refresh token today; any future rotating artefact): rotate N times, then present generation k<N and assert BOTH that the call fails AND that every live credential of that grant — the access token from generation N and the refresh token from generation N — is dead afterwards (verifyAccessToken rejects, a further exchangeRefreshToken rejects). Parameterize over N in {1,2,5} and over which generation is replayed, so a fix that only revokes the immediately-previous generation is caught too.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `private revokeGrant(grantId)` (which already walks both access and refresh by grantId), `sweep()`'s existing `expiresAtMs < nowMs` loops, and the PROVIDER_STORES / class-doc ratchets that will demand the new Map be classified.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A legitimate client that replays a refresh token after its rotation response was lost in transit (a dropped 200) today gets invalid_grant with the grant still alive; with the fix it destroys the grant, and in this single-tenant design that means the owner must re-enter the passphrase at /parley/consent. RFC 9700 accepts this cost explicitly; it is nonetheless a real usability regression on a flaky link and must be stated, not hidden.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: I prototyped exactly this in the worktree and ran the suite: 3 tests failed, all inventory ratchets and none behavioural — oauth-provider.test.ts 'classifies every Map the provider actually keeps', 'the class doc names retired', and 'CLIENT_STATES covers every client-keyed store the provider declares'. remote.test.ts:382 and the revocation-chain table at oauth-provider.test.ts:761 both still passed.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while a different theft path remains (e.g. an access token leaked without its refresh token), the stolen access token still lives out its 1h TTL — this fix addresses reuse of the refresh credential only. It does not hide the symptom: without it, a stolen refresh token is undetectable by construction.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two concurrent /token refresh calls with the same R1 on the single event loop: the first `this.refresh.get(R1)` hit runs to completion synchronously through revokeGrant+issue before the second handler resumes, so the second sees R1 only in `retired` and revokes the grant — which is the specified behaviour for a genuine double-submit, and is also why the newlyRejects note above matters.

The two auth-layer calls are dead: they re-set `env` to a value it already has and register a second `terminalErrorHandler` behind one that always terminates.

That catches both the current duplication and the opposite regression where a new door installs it zero times, which the present suite would also miss for any door not listed in DOORS.

I also checked that no test imports hardenErrorSurface from remote.ts/oidc-remote.ts; error-surface.test.ts imports it directly from ./error-surface.js.

summary: OidcTokenVerifier is re-exported from src/index.ts:126 but its constructor asserts nothing. Every invariant createOidcRemoteApp enforces — assertTrustRootUrl on the JWKS URL, the 0..300 clock-skew bound, and the 'at least one identity gate' rule — lives in invariants.ts, which is NOT exported. The package's own hygiene.test.ts states the rule it is breaking: 'A symbol the barrel re-exports is something an operator can call directly, so the config schema's rules are not in front of it — whatever guards it must live in the function.'
failure: `new OidcTokenVerifier({ issuer: 'https://kc.example/realms/r', audience: 'parley-mcp', jwksUri: 'http://kc.example/realms/r/protocol/openid-connect/certs' })` constructs and fetches its trust root over plaintext HTTP — anyone on the path substitutes their own JWKS and mints tokens this verifier accepts. The same constructor with no allowedSubjects/allowedUsernames/requiredRole admits every user of the realm, and with `clockSkewS: 86_400` accepts tokens a day past exp. All three are refused at boot when the identical policy arrives through createOidcRemoteApp/createRemoteAuthApp, so which of two documented entry points an integrator picks decides whether the guards exist.
remediation: Move the two value-independent checks into the constructor: call `assertTrustRootUrl(opts.jwksUri, 'OidcVerifierOptions.jwksUri')` and bound clockSkewS to an integer in 0..300 (reusing MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_S). For the identity gate, do not silently require one — make it explicit in the type (a discriminated `gates` option, or a mandatory `allowAnyRealmUser: true` opt-in) so a gate-less verifier is a deliberate, visible choice rather than a default.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a factory enforces an invariant that its exported building block does not'. Extend hygiene.test.ts's 'every public auth entry point is driven by the offline suite' into an invariant-parity table: for each (barrel-exported constructor/factory, invariant in invariants.ts) pair, assert the violating input is refused by BOTH the factory and the block — driven off the exported symbol list and the exported assert* names so a new invariant or a new export joins automatically. The existing invariants.test.ts rows only ever go through createOidcRemoteApp, which is why the gap reads as coverage.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: invariants.ts `assertTrustRootUrl` (its `parsed.protocol !== 'https:' && !LOOPBACK_HOSTS.has(parsed.hostname)` branch, which permits the http://127.0.0.1 JWKS every test fake serves) and MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_S = 300.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A direct `new OidcTokenVerifier({ jwksUri: 'http://kc.example/...' })` against a non-loopback plaintext JWKS, and any clockSkewS outside 0..300 or non-integer. Both are already rejected via the factory path.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: I applied the jwksUri + clockSkewS half in the worktree and ran the full auth suite: 15 files, 1145/1145 pass — every fake IdP uses http://127.0.0.1, which assertTrustRootUrl exempts, and every clockSkewS in the suite is 1/30/120. The identity-gate half is different and I did NOT apply it: oidc-verifier.test.ts, oidc-token-kinds.test.ts and oidc-verifier-wiring.test.ts all construct gate-less verifiers (`new OidcTokenVerifier({ issuer, audience: AUD, jwksUri })`), so requiring a gate in the constructor would fail roughly 40 rows and those fixtures must be updated with the explicit opt-in.

summary: 'Token lifetime, refresh, and revocation are Keycloak's: Parley honors `exp` on every request...' reads as: revoking a session or token in Keycloak cuts the bridge off. OidcTokenVerifier does purely local JWT validation — no introspection (RFC 7662), no revocation list — so a token revoked at the IdP keeps working until `exp + clock_skew_s`. The neighbouring bullet 'Keep both Keycloak and Parley behind TLS; the token is a bearer credential' reinforces the reading that the IdP is the live authority.
failure: Mint a Keycloak access token for the bridge, revoke the user's session (or the token) at the realm, and POST to /mcp with that bearer inside its exp window: verifyAccessToken succeeds — jwtVerify only checks signature/iss/aud/exp/nbf and the gates read from the token's own claims — and the request is served. With the doc's own recommended 5-minute lifetime that is up to 5 minutes plus clock_skew_s (default 30s, configurable to 300s) of access after revocation; an operator who raised the realm's access-token lifetime widens it proportionally.
remediation: State the mechanism: 'Parley validates tokens locally and does not call the introspection endpoint, so a token revoked at Keycloak stays accepted until its `exp` (plus `clock_skew_s`). Keep the realm's access-token lifetime short — the default 5 minutes bounds the window — and treat `clock_skew_s` as widening it.' Line 40's bullet list ('signature via JWKS / iss / exp / nbf / aud / claim gates') should also say that revocation is not among the checks.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a security doc names a control the verifier does not perform'. Parameterize a doc-vs-code table over the checks OidcTokenVerifier actually runs: derive the claim set the verifier reads (issuer, audience, exp, nbf, scope, sub, preferred_username, realm_access.roles) and assert that every security bullet in docs/keycloak-integration.md that names a validation names one of them — with an explicit deny row for 'revocation'/'introspection'. That also catches the next doc paragraph that promises a check nobody wired up.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: oidc-verifier.ts:118-125 — the single jwtVerify call is the whole validation, and nothing else in the class performs a network call after construction; `expiresAt: payload.exp + skewS` at line 159 sets the outer bound.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — hygiene.test.ts's doc scanner only grades paragraphs that name an *.e2e.test.ts file and mention skipping, so this paragraph is outside every existing doc assertion. I grepped all *.test.ts under packages/bridge-core/src/auth for 'revocation' and 'introspect': the only hits are the built-in AS's RFC 7009 endpoint tests, which are a different mode.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Doc-only. If the bug being described is 'operators believe revocation is immediate', the doc fix removes the false belief but leaves the exposure window itself; closing that would require introspection or shorter exp, which is a separate design decision.

summary: `evictionCandidate` decides liveness with `state.expiresAtMs >= nowMs`, which is the correct complement of the provider's own expiry test (`expiresAtMs < nowMs` in sweep(), challengeForAuthorizationCode, exchangeAuthorizationCode and exchangeRefreshToken). Nothing grades the boundary: the whole eviction suite runs on clocks far from any expiry.

The provider injects its clock, so the tuple is exactly reachable and deterministic in a test.

Assert that a record at exactly `now` is uniformly LIVE across all of them, so the sites cannot drift apart. The existing DCR-cap suite (oauth-provider.test.ts:1076-1334) is too narrow because every row runs at a fixed clock nowhere near a TTL edge.
