summary: When neither the JOSE header nor the claims carry a `typ`, isAccessToken falls back to `ID_TOKEN_ONLY_CLAIMS.every((claim) => payload[claim] === undefined)` — i.e. absence of nonce/at_hash/c_hash is treated as proof of being an access token. OIDC Core makes `nonce` conditional on the request and `at_hash`/`c_hash` conditional on the flow, so a plain authorization-code ID token from a typ-less IdP carries none of the three and is admitted. The behaviour is deliberate and pinned (oidc-token-kinds.test.ts KIND_MATRIX row 'neither nonce nor at_hash' expects accept for 'no typ at all'), so this is a challenge to the adjudication, not an unnoticed bug.
failure: With a typ-less IdP and an operator who sets `auth.oidc.audience` to the connector's client_id — a natural choice for IdPs that put the client_id in `aud`, and one nothing in the config schema or invariants.ts warns against — a client's own ID token satisfies signature, iss, aud and exp, carries no ID-only claim, and is accepted as authorization for /mcp. An ID token is a login receipt the client already holds (and which leaks into browser history/fragments in hybrid flows), so it becomes a bearer credential for the bridge. I did not reproduce this end to end: it needs a typ-less IdP fixture and an audience==client_id config, neither of which exists in the suite, hence PLAUSIBLE.
remediation: Do not widen the heuristic — narrow the configuration around it. Either (a) refuse at boot when `auth.oidc.audience` equals a value the IdP would also place in an ID token's `aud`, which is not decidable in general, so instead (b) require a positive access-token signal when the deployment can supply one: add an opt-in `require_typed_access_token: true` that makes ACCESS_TOKEN_TYPES membership mandatory, and recommend it in docs/keycloak-integration.md for any IdP that stamps `typ` (Keycloak always does). Leave the current fallback as the default so typ-less IdPs still work.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a kind discriminator that reads absence as affirmation'. Extend the existing KIND_MATRIX with an audience axis: for each (typ value, ID-only-claim shape) cell, run once with `audience` = the resource id and once with `audience` = the token's `azp`/client_id, and assert the verdict is identical. Add a row for a typ-less ID token minted with an `aud` equal to the configured audience and a `nonce`-free code flow — the cell that today distinguishes 'we cannot tell' from 'we decided it is fine'.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: isAccessToken's ordering (NON_ACCESS_TOKEN_TYPES first, then ACCESS_TOKEN_TYPES, then the claim-shape fallback) and the fact that jose has already enforced iss/aud/exp before it runs, so the fallback is the only remaining discriminator.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Under the opt-in flag, every token from an IdP that stamps no `typ` anywhere — which is why it must be opt-in and not the default.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none as an opt-in; if the flag were made the default, the four KIND_MATRIX cells expecting accept for 'no typ at all' and the ASYMMETRIC algorithm rows in oidc-token-kinds.test.ts (whose mint() stamps no typ) would all fail — 14+ rows.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the operator still sets audience == client_id, an IdP that does stamp typ is protected and a typ-less one is unchanged unless the flag is set. It does not fix the underlying ambiguity, which is unfixable from the token alone; it moves the decision to the operator.

summary: `plaintextCredentialOrigin` decides "does this DSN carry a credential" from the DSN string only, while `usesDefaultCredentials` twelve lines below deliberately falls back to PGUSER/PGPASSWORD because "the parser reports a credential the DSN omits as '', and pg authenticates such a DSN as PGUSER/PGPASSWORD". So the one warning that exists to stop a password crossing the network in the clear is silent for exactly the credential placement CLAUDE.md prescribes (.env).
failure: `PGUSER=app PGPASSWORD=hunter2` in the environment, `backend_config.url: 'postgres://db.example.com/prod'` (no sslmode). Reproduced in-tree: `plaintextCredentialOrigin(url)` returns `undefined`, so `connect()` prints nothing, and pg then sends `hunter2` and every message body to a remote host with TLS off. The same DSN written as `postgres://app:hunter2@db.example.com/prod` prints the SECURITY line. `creds-warning.test.ts` row `['no credential to lose', 'postgres://db.example.com/prod', false]` positively asserts the silence.
remediation: Mirror the env fallback the sibling function already documents: `const carriesCredential = (parsed.user || process.env['PGUSER'] || '') !== '' || (parsed.password || process.env['PGPASSWORD'] || '') !== '';`. Keep the origin (host:port) as the only thing named, unchanged.
testUpgrade: The class is "a credential-bearing setting pg honours that this plugin's screen reads from only one of its two sources". Turn TRANSPORT_CASES into a matrix of (credential source) x (host spelling) x (ssl setting), where credential source is a table row — {in userinfo}, {in libpq query params}, {in PGUSER/PGPASSWORD}, {in PGPASSFILE}, {none anywhere} — and assert the warning fires iff the effective credential is non-empty AND the host is not provably loopback AND pg would not encrypt. Drive the credential-source list from the same list `usesDefaultCredentials` consults, so a source added to one screen is graded against the other automatically. The existing `['no credential to lose', …, false]` row is the one too narrow to have caught this, and ENV_CASES already proves the suite knows about the env source but applies it to only one of the two screens.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `parse` from pg-connection-string 2.14.0 (already imported), and the existing early-return branch `if (!carriesCredential || host === '' || isLoopbackHost(host) || Boolean(parsed.ssl)) return undefined;` — only the first disjunct changes. `isLoopbackHost` and the `ssl` test are untouched.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — no DSN that warns today stops warning.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `{ url: 'postgres://db.example.com/prod' }` with PGPASSWORD set now prints the plaintext SECURITY line to stderr, where today it prints nothing.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: `packages/bridge-postgres/test/creds-warning.test.ts > 'Postgres plaintext-credential warning classifies the transport, not the scheme' > 'no credential to lose'` will fail whenever PGUSER or PGPASSWORD is set in the ambient environment. That file's earlier ENV_CASES describe calls `vi.stubEnv('PGUSER'/'PGPASSWORD', …)` and vitest.config.ts sets no `unstubEnvs`, so the last ENV case's stub (PGUSER='parley') plausibly leaks forward into TRANSPORT_CASES in the same file — I did not run the patched code to confirm the leak, so that row likely needs an explicit `vi.stubEnv('PGUSER','')`/`vi.stubEnv('PGPASSWORD','')` alongside the fix. No other test calls `plaintextCredentialOrigin`.

Nothing about the connection itself changes either way — this is a warning and not a load error, which is the documented and correct choice for the loopback dev server.

summary: `TEARDOWN_GUARD_SITES = 21` pins the exact number of regex matches for a teardown guard across all of `src/**`. It counts guards, not guarded awaits, so it is green for the failure it exists to catch and red for the refactor it should permit — both of the failure modes CLAUDE.md's standing rule on architectural tests names ("a split blocked", "a probe turned tautology").
failure: Demonstrated both directions in this worktree. (a) Adding `await this.require().query('SELECT 1');` inside `readPage` between `assertCursor` and `readSince` — a new teardown-crossing await with no guard after it — leaves the census at 21 and the test PASSES. (b) Extracting `protected stale(epoch: number) { return this.stopped || epoch !== this.epoch; }` into state.ts and calling it from the two identical guards in push.ts — behaviour-identical, one named predicate instead of two duplicated conditions — drops the count to 20 and the test FAILS with 'a guard site was added or removed'. The census blocks a strictly better shape while admitting the defect.
remediation: Delete the count pin and grade the invariant instead: enumerate, from SOURCE, every method that captures `const <x> = this.epoch` (or publishes into `this.starting`), and for each `await` in that method's body assert a guard appears before the next assignment to `this.*` or the next handler/resolve call. That is the property; the number of guards is not. If a census is kept at all, assert `guards >= teardownCrossingAwaits` rather than `guards === 21`, so consolidation is allowed and an unguarded await is not.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a source-text census pinned by exact count". Add a meta-rule over `packages/bridge-postgres/test/**` that fails any `toBe(<integer literal>)` whose subject is derived from SOURCE or from a `readFileSync` of `src/**`, and require such rules to be expressed as an inequality or as a derived-from-the-same-source equality. Pair it with two self-check cases the way suite-hygiene.test.ts already does elsewhere: one sample where the rule must fire (a consolidated guard) and one where it must not (an added unguarded await must be RED). The existing TEARDOWN_GUARD_FORMS table is too narrow — it only proves the regex can see each spelling, never that the census direction is right.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: SOURCE from test/sources.ts (concatenated `src/**` text) and the existing TEARDOWN_GUARD regex, both of which stay. The replacement needs no new plumbing — the same string is already available.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A refactor that replaces N duplicated `this.stopped || epoch !== this.epoch` conditions with one named predicate (proved RED today).
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A new `await` inside an epoch-capturing method with no re-check between it and the next mutation of plugin state (proved GREEN today).
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: `lifecycle.test.ts > a chore in flight when disconnect lands never touches the next lifecycle > every teardown guard in the source is represented by a row above` — the test being replaced. I did not exhaustively enumerate every other consumer of SOURCE in this package, so a second rule in lifecycle.test.ts reading the same constant is possible; TEARDOWN_GUARD_FORMS itself is independent of the count and keeps passing.

The behavioural CROSS_CELLS table is what actually protects the five chores today; the census adds no coverage on top of it.

summary: `subs`, `waiters`, `subscribing` and `listens` are keyed by `channelFor(topic)` = `parley_<md5(topic)>` — a truncating, cryptographically broken digest — rather than by the topic. The digest is legitimately the wire channel (it has to fit 63 bytes and byte-match the trigger), but using it as the in-process identity of a subscription silently merges two topics that collide.
failure: Given two allowlisted topics A and B with md5(A) == md5(B) (MD5 chosen-prefix collisions are constructible in hours, and a topic is free-form text): `subscribe(A, hA)` registers `subs[c] = {topic: A, handlers:[hA]}`. `subscribe(B, hB)` then takes the fast path at index.ts:364 — `const live = this.subs.get(channel); if (live !== undefined) { live.handlers.push(hB); return; }` — resolves successfully, and from then on `drain` reads `WHERE topic = A` and delivers A's messages to hB, while every message posted to B is never delivered on the live path. subscribe() reports success for a live path that does not exist. Reachability is gated by the operator's topic list, so this is latent rather than agent-triggerable.
remediation: Key the participant registries by topic and keep the digest as a derived label: `subs: Map<Topic, TopicSubscription>` and `subscribing: Map<Topic, …>`, plus `channelTopics: Map<string, Set<Topic>>`; `redrive(channel)` resolves the channel to its topic set and drives each. `listens` may stay channel-keyed — a shared LISTEN for colliding topics is harmless, because every drain and every recheck re-queries by topic. No schema or wire change is required.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a derived label used as an identity key". Add a parameterized case that stubs `channelFor` to return a CONSTANT for every topic (or to collide two fresh topics), then asserts, for N distinct topics: each subscribe gets its own TopicSubscription carrying its own `topic`; each handler sees only its own topic's messages; and N independent blocking fetchRecents each wake on their own topic. Parameterize over N = 2, 3. That one stub also catches the next registry keyed on a digest. Today's subscribe-race.test.ts and waiters.test.ts only ever use distinct-digest topics, so no existing case can observe this.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `redrive(channels, doorbell)` at listener.ts:107, which today does `this.subs.get(channel)` and `this.waiters.get(channel)`; both lookups become channel -> topics -> participants. `releaseListen(channel, entry)` in listen.ts stays channel-keyed and unchanged.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `subscribe(B, hB)` after `subscribe(A, hA)` when md5(A)==md5(B) now builds a second, correct subscription instead of silently joining A's.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: waiters.test.ts imports channelFor but asserts against state.established/state.unlistened, which are LISTEN-level and unaffected. connection-hygiene.test.ts uses registrySizes() (sizes only, identical for distinct topics). The at-risk ones are any case doing a keyed lookup into priv.subs/priv.waiters — I did not read subscribe-race.test.ts or teardown-delivery.test.ts line-by-line, so check those two before applying.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the cross-wiring completely. If instead only the digest were widened (e.g. truncated sha256), the collision probability drops but the structural defect — subscription identity is not the topic — remains, and the wire channel would have to change on both sides of the trigger, which is a compatibility break this fix avoids entirely.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two concurrent `subscribe` calls on colliding topics: the `subscribing` in-flight map is also channel-keyed, so it must move to the topic key with the others, or the second caller awaits the first's promise and receives the wrong TopicSubscription. That is the one interleaving the fix must not miss. A NOTIFY landing between the two registrations drives `redrive(channel)` over the topic set, so both drains run.

summary: The listener reconnect loop uses `delay(RECONNECT_DELAY_MS)` from @sharptrick/parley-net-util, which is `new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms))` — a bare, ref'd timer — re-armed forever while `!this.stopped`, each iteration also dialling a new ref'd Client socket. Both the prune timer (index.ts:153) and the drain re-drain timer (push.ts:100) carry an explicit `.unref()` with a comment stating the invariant: "a leaked-but-never-disconnect()ed plugin cannot by itself pin the event loop". This path violates that stated invariant. The constant is also named a "backoff" while being a fixed 500ms interval, unbounded in count and total time.
failure: Plugin connected, `subscribe()` established, database becomes permanently unreachable, and the host process drops its reference to the plugin without calling `disconnect()` (or a supervisor that never wires SIGTERM). `reconnectListener` loops forever at 500ms; the ref'd setTimeout plus the ref'd dial socket keep the Node event loop alive, so the process never exits on its own — the exact outcome the two `.unref()` comments say is not allowed. Traced by reading packages/bridge-net-util/src/timing.ts:2 and the `while (!this.stopped && epoch === this.epoch)` loop.
remediation: Use a locally unref'd sleep in this loop only — `await new Promise<void>((r) => { setTimeout(r, RECONNECT_DELAY_MS).unref(); })` — rather than changing `delay` in the shared @sharptrick/parley-net-util, which other backends depend on. Separately, either grow the interval (500ms doubling to a ceiling, matching push.ts's DRAIN_RETRY_CEILING_MS shape) or rename the constant to RECONNECT_INTERVAL_MS so the name stops claiming a backoff there is not.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a plugin-owned repeating timer or retry loop that is not unref'd". Add a rule over `src/**` that finds every setTimeout/setInterval/delay(/sleep( reachable from a loop or a re-arming callback and requires an `.unref()` on the same expression or an entry in an explicit allowlist pinned by value — and pair it with a runtime case that spawns a child process which connects, subscribes, loses its peer, drops the reference without disconnecting, and asserts the child exits within a budget. That runtime case also covers the prune and re-drain timers, so the three stop being three hand-written `.unref()`s nobody re-checks.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `delay` is imported at listener.ts:1 and used at exactly one site (line 155); replacing it there removes the import. Nothing else in this package calls it.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at the seam.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None from the unref alone — the timer still fires identically under a running event loop, and vitest's loop is always ref'd by the runner. Changing the CADENCE is different: connection-hygiene.test.ts sleeps 505ms to land inside the backoff (the 'reconnect, disconnect in-flight' and 'settled' rows) and lifecycle.test.ts's 'reconnect-backoff' chore times off the same 500ms, so a doubling backoff would break those. That is why the unref and the cadence should be separated.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: The unref fixes the pin. If applied while the cadence stays fixed, a permanently-down database still costs two dials per second forever — cheap, but unbounded, and undocumented in the README.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two callers on the new path: a subscribe and a blocking fetchRecent both awaiting `ensureListener` during the same backoff are unaffected — the sleep is internal to the reconnect loop and neither caller's promise changes. A disconnect() landing inside the unref'd sleep behaves exactly as today: the timer still fires, the loop re-reads stopped/epoch and returns.

summary: `resolveIdentity` reads `SELECT backend_ref … WHERE handle = $1`, and on a miss issues `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (handle) DO NOTHING` and returns `{ handle, backendRef: handle }` without re-reading. If another session inserts an operator row between the two statements, the DO NOTHING correctly preserves it but the caller is handed `handle`, which is not what the store holds — contradicting the README's "an operator may pre-register a handle with a `backend_ref` of their own and `resolveIdentity` returns that instead of echoing the handle".
failure: Process A: `resolveIdentity('alice')` -> SELECT returns no row. Concurrently an operator (or a second bridge) runs `INSERT INTO <table>_senders VALUES ('alice','@alice:matrix.org')`. A's `INSERT … DO NOTHING` no-ops and A returns `{handle:'alice', backendRef:'alice'}` while the store holds '@alice:matrix.org'. Postgres is the explicitly multi-process backend, and this is the only seam call whose answer is derived from a read the plugin then does not re-validate against the write it issues.
remediation: Collapse the two statements into one on the read path: `INSERT INTO <senders> (handle, backend_ref) VALUES ($1,$1) ON CONFLICT (handle) DO UPDATE SET backend_ref = <senders>.backend_ref RETURNING backend_ref`, and return the returned value. The self-assigning DO UPDATE is the standard idiom that makes ON CONFLICT always RETURN a row. Keep post()'s registerSender on DO NOTHING: it runs on every write and a self-update would create a dead tuple per post.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a seam answer derived from a read the plugin does not re-validate against its own write". Add a parameterized case that, for each of resolveIdentity's arms, interleaves a competing writer at the exact seam: rows {handle absent, operator row inserted BETWEEN the select and the insert}, {handle absent, nothing competing}, {handle present}. Force the interleaving deterministically with a fake pool whose SELECT resolution is held open while an admin INSERT lands (pg-harness already exports `withAdmin`), and assert in every row that the returned backendRef equals what a fresh `SELECT backend_ref` reports. `sender-registry.test.ts > 'never overwrites an operator row'` is too narrow — it grades the stored row, not the value handed back under a race.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `this.require().query(...)` and the `<table>_senders (handle TEXT PRIMARY KEY, backend_ref TEXT NOT NULL)` schema at schema.ts:130 — the PK is the arbiter index `ON CONFLICT (handle)` needs, and it exists. The `serverRefused` wrapper around the try stays.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — the same handles are accepted; only the returned backendRef changes, and only in the racing case.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: I did not read sender-registry.test.ts line-by-line. Its ORIGINS table is described as 'read, written, and never overwrites an operator row', which the self-assigning DO UPDATE preserves — but if any row asserts that a hit performs NO write (by counting queries, or by checking xmin/ctid stability), it will fail, because DO UPDATE writes a new row version. That is the one place to check before applying.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes it. If applied to post()'s registerSender instead of to resolveIdentity, nothing is fixed and every post pays a row-version write — strictly worse.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two concurrent `resolveIdentity('alice')` on a fresh handle: both issue the single statement, one inserts and one takes the DO UPDATE arm, and both RETURN the same backend_ref. That is the interleaving today's code gets wrong only when the competing writer is an operator; the single statement makes both cases identical.

Repair the CLI sentence to "…since that default names a different deployment's database url, table, handle and topic allowlist." That form also catches the next rule stated in prose and enforced only in code.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None, provided the two byte-count substrings survive the rewording. suite-hygiene.test.ts's REVIEWER_DIRECTED patterns (/\ba reviewer\b/i, /[\w-]+\/[\w.-]*\.test\.ts/, …) must not be introduced by the new prose — the replacement wording above introduces none of them.

summary: The single invariant CLAUDE.md states as a prime rule — never order on `timestamp` — is asserted only in a comment. Rewriting `SQL.selectAfter` from `ORDER BY id ASC` to `ORDER BY ts ASC, id ASC` leaves all 767 tests green on both drivers, including the whole conformance suite and the query-plan assertion that derives its SQL from this very map. Every test posts through `post()`, whose `ts` is monotonic with the rowid, so no case can distinguish the two keys. The README simultaneously documents that this store DOES hold rows whose `ts` disagrees with rowid order ('a peer whose host clock runs 2 h behind writes rows that a 1 h window deletes ... whatever rowid they hold'), so the disagreeing case is a stated deployment, not a hypothetical.
failure: Reproduced. Topic `ctx` holding three rows written by peers with skewed clocks — rowid 1 ts=12:00, rowid 2 ts=10:00, rowid 3 ts=11:00 — paged with `fetchRecent({topic, since:'<storeId>.0', limit:2})` then re-paged on the returned cursor. Correct code yields first/second/third. With `ORDER BY ts ASC, id ASC` the first page returns rowids 2,3 and `nextCursor` = `<storeId>.3`; the second page is empty and paging stops, so rowid 1 is dropped permanently and core's read-state is advanced past it. The suite stays 767/767 green through that change.
remediation: Add a guard that plants rows whose `ts` order disagrees with their rowid order (bypassing `post()`, via the same `(p as unknown as { driver }).driver.prepare(...)` cast the rest of `test/` already uses) and asserts, for the resuming arm and the since-less arm and the live poll loop, that (a) every planted row is served exactly once across paging to exhaustion, (b) the served order is rowid order, and (c) `nextCursor` equals the maximum rowid served. Do not change product code — it is correct today; the defect is that nothing holds it there.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a read path's sort/limit key silently becomes something other than the rowid'. Parameterize over {selectAfter (resuming), selectRecent (since-less), the subscribe poll loop} x {limit 1,2,3,all} x a generated permutation of `ts` values that is independent of insertion order (include equal-`ts` ties, a strictly-descending `ts`, and a single far-past outlier). Assert the multiset of contents equals the planted set, the sequence equals rowid order, and nextCursor == max(rowid served). A widened generator that shuffles `ts` also catches a future `ORDER BY ts DESC` in `selectRecent`, an `ORDER BY` dropped entirely, and a `predecessor` statement re-keyed on `ts`. `test/background-jobs.test.ts`'s `${name} resolves through an index, not a table scan` is the existing test closest to this and is too narrow: it passed under the mutation because it only looks for the index name in the plan and never grades the sort key. `test/retention-window.test.ts` already knows how to plant skewed `ts` rows and is the natural place to borrow the fixture from.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `SqliteCatchUp.fetchRecent`'s resuming arm (`resumeAfter !== undefined` branch, `this.require(this.selectAfterStmt).all(args.topic, resumeAfter, limit)`) and the exposed-for-tests `driver` field on the plugin instance. I used the since-less arm first only to mint a `<storeId>.0` floor cursor; that arm's cold-start horizon (it serves the newest `limit` window, not the oldest) is why a naive version of this test fails against correct code — my first attempt did exactly that and I corrected it.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Any future edit that makes `SQL.selectAfter`/`selectRecent` order or truncate a page by anything other than the rowid, including `ORDER BY ts ASC, id ASC`, which today ships green.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I ran the added test alongside the package suite; it is a new file touching no shared fixture and no product source. summary: `retention prune error visibility` calls `holder.prune()` exactly once per case, so every piece of state that only exists across invocations is ungraded. Four independent mutations to `SqliteRetention.prune` and `SqlitePlugin.connect` leave the suite 766/766 green: deleting `this.pruneFailures = 0` (the reset that gives `#N` its 'consecutive' meaning), deleting `|| this.pruneFailures === 1` (the first-failure-after-recovery-is-loud arm), deleting `this.lastPruneDiag = now` (the rate limiter's only write), and deleting connect()'s reset of both fields. The equivalent poll-loop logic IS graded — `test/subscription-health.test.ts`'s 'the first unavailable tick after a successful read is loud, even behind a lock burst' turns red when I delete poll.ts's `diagQuietUntil = 0`. The asymmetry is the finding; the README explicitly says the prune 'reports failures the same way'.
failure: Delete line 23 of packages/bridge-sqlite/src/retention.ts (`this.pruneFailures = 0;`). Suite: 766 passed. A prune that fails, succeeds, then fails again now writes `retention prune failed (#2)` where the shipped code writes `(#1)`, and an operator reading `#7` cannot tell a seven-hour outage from seven scattered ones. Delete line 31's `|| this.pruneFailures === 1` instead: same green, and a failure recurring within a minute of a recovery is now silent. Delete line 32's `this.lastPruneDiag = now`: same green, and the rate limiter never suppresses anything ever again.
remediation: Turn the single `holder.prune()` into a scripted sequence per row of the existing ERROR_CASES table — fail, fail, succeed, fail — driven by a mutable flag on the swapped `pruneStmt.run`, and assert after each step: the `#N` in the emitted line, that the counter returns to 1 after a success, that the first failure after a success is emitted even when `lastPruneDiag` is recent (freeze the clock with `vi.setSystemTime` so the 60 s arm cannot mask it), and that a second failure inside the same minute is suppressed. Keep the lock-classed row asserting zero lines throughout.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'rate-limited, counted background-job diagnostics graded by a single invocation'. Make it one parameterized table shared by both background jobs (poll tick and retention prune), rows = (error class sequence) x (clock advance between steps), columns = expected consecutive-failure count, expected emitted-line count, expected health state. Driving both jobs from one table is what makes the asymmetry impossible to reintroduce: today poll.ts's ladder has `test/subscription-health.test.ts`'s 'no interleaving of error classes launders the escalation ladder' (which is thorough) and prune has one call.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The existing fixture's `holder.pruneStmt = { all, get, run }` swap and `holder.prune()` direct call — both already used at background-jobs.test.ts:334-342 — plus `vi.setSystemTime`, needed because `lastPruneDiag` starts at 0 so the `now - 0 > DIAG_INTERVAL_MS` arm is true on the first failure and would mask the `pruneFailures === 1` arm.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A prune whose failure counter is not per-consecutive-run, whose first-failure-after-recovery is silent, or whose rate limiter never advances its watermark.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. The change is confined to the body of `retention prune error visibility`; I checked that no other file reads `pruneFailures` or `lastPruneDiag` (grep across src/ and test/ finds them only in retention.ts, index.ts and this describe block).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is hidden — the product code is currently correct, so this only removes the ability to break it unnoticed. Note the overlap with the next finding: if the rate limiter is removed as dead machinery, the rows asserting suppression must go with it rather than being kept as a test of code that no longer exists.

summary: README: 'The retention prune reports failures the same way (quiet for lock contention, a rate-limited stderr line otherwise)', where 'the same way' points at the poll loop's 'rate-limited to about one line a minute per topic'. The prune's rate limiter can never suppress a line. `prune()` has exactly two callers: `connect()` (once) and `setInterval(..., PRUNE_INTERVAL_MS = 3_600_000)`. The self-rescheduling `pruneBatchTimer` at line 27 sits on the success path only — a failing prune returns from the catch without rescheduling. So consecutive prunes are always at least an hour apart and `now - this.lastPruneDiag > DIAG_INTERVAL_MS (60_000)` is unconditionally true, making both `lastPruneDiag` and the `|| this.pruneFailures === 1` disjunct incapable of changing the outcome. A reader takes them as load-bearing; `test/readme-claims.test.ts` pins the sentence's presence but never checks it against the code.
failure: Input: a store whose retention prune fails every time (read-only mount). Documented output: 'about one line a minute', with suppression in between. Actual output: exactly one line per hour, one per connect — the same line count with the limiter deleted. Confirmed by mutation: deleting `this.lastPruneDiag = now;` changes nothing observable and the suite stays 766/766 green.
remediation: Prefer the doc fix: replace 'the same way' with what prune actually does — 'one line per failing prune, at most one per hour because that is the prune cadence; the first failure is always loud'. If instead the machinery is kept, give it a reason to exist by making the batch chain retry on a recoverable failure, at which point the limiter becomes reachable and the previous finding's test must cover it. Do NOT delete `pruneFailures` itself — it carries the `#N` counter the operator reads.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a documented mitigation whose trigger condition the code can never reach'. `test/readme-claims.test.ts` currently grades only that a sentence is PRESENT in the README; widen it so a row may carry an executable predicate over the code as well as a regex over the prose — e.g. for the rate-limit row, drive the job at its real cadence with a frozen clock and assert the emitted-line count matches the documented rate. Parameterize over both background jobs so the poll loop (where the limiter IS reachable) and the prune (where it is not) are graded by the same row shape and the divergence has to be declared.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The two-caller analysis: `index.ts:67` `this.prune()` and `index.ts:71` `setInterval(() => this.prune(), PRUNE_INTERVAL_MS)`, plus `retention.ts:27` `if (Number(info.changes) >= PRUNE_BATCH) this.pruneBatchTimer = setTimeout(...)` sitting inside the `try`, after the statement that would have thrown. That last branch is the whole dependency: if a future change reschedules the batch chain on a caught failure, the limiter becomes live and a doc-only fix would then be wrong.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — a doc edit changes no accepted input.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: `test/readme-claims.test.ts` has no row matching /rate-limited/ or /one line a minute/ today, so editing that sentence breaks nothing. I checked the CLAIMS table: the closest rows are 'that a lock-classed poll failure is quiet but still counted' (/without a stderr line/) and the backoff row, neither of which touches the prune sentence.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the doc is corrected and the dead limiter is left in place, an operator's expectation is fixed but ~4 lines of unreachable code and one unreachable field remain, which is exactly the shape that made the previous finding's mutations invisible. If the code is deleted instead and the batch chain is later made to retry on failure, the flood the limiter existed to prevent returns with nothing guarding it.

summary: `subscribe`'s JSDoc justifies sampling the tail for an evicted topic with: 'Sampling is right only for a topic catch-up never read — or one whose hand-off point aged out of CATCHUP_LEDGER_MAX: its rows are history the live path has never owned.' `test/bounded-state.test.ts`'s row 'one topic past full, this topic recorded first' pins `pushed: []` — a message posted AFTER that topic's catch-up and BEFORE its subscribe is not delivered. Those rows are not history the live path never owned; they are precisely the hand-off-window rows the ledger exists to protect, and the JSDoc's own first paragraph says rows in that window are 'owned by neither path'. The eviction reopens the gap the surrounding code closes, silently, for the first-caught-up topics. The README documents neither the ledger, its 1024 bound, nor this loss.
failure: Traced through core: `transport/stdio-bridge.ts:76` runs `catchUpAll` over `allow.topics()` to completion, then `transport/push-loop.ts:68` subscribes each in the same order. With more than CATCHUP_LEDGER_MAX (1024) configured topics, topic #1's hand-off point is evicted by topic #1025's `recordCatchUp` before `subscribe(topic #1)` runs. `subscribe` then falls back to `this.maxId(topic)`. Any message a peer committed to topic #1 during the catch-up of topics 2..1025 is above the cursor core persisted and below the sampled mark, so it is pushed by nobody for the life of the process. `test/bounded-state.test.ts` reproduces the plugin-level shape directly and asserts the loss as intended.
remediation: Two separable parts. (1) Correct the JSDoc: say that an evicted topic's `subscribe` samples the tail and that messages committed in that topic's hand-off window are therefore left to the next catch-up rather than pushed. (2) Surface the bound where an operator meets it: add CATCHUP_LEDGER_MAX and its consequence to the README's config section, and emit one stderr line the first time an eviction happens while any topic is still unsubscribed. Do not raise the cap — the bound is correct; it is the silence that is not.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a bounded internal cache whose eviction silently degrades a delivery guarantee'. Add a row to `test/bounded-state.test.ts`'s EVICTION table that asserts the OBSERVABLE signal (a stderr line naming the evicted topic), not just the message set, and parameterize the whole table over the number of topics {LEDGER_MAX-1, LEDGER_MAX, LEDGER_MAX+1, 4*LEDGER_MAX} x {evicted-before-subscribe, evicted-after-subscribe} so a future change to the eviction policy has to restate which arm loses messages. Pair it with an assertion in `test/readme-claims.test.ts` that the README states the bound, so the cap cannot be raised or lowered without the prose moving.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `SqliteCatchUp.recordCatchUp`'s eviction loop (`while (this.caughtUpThrough.size > CATCHUP_LEDGER_MAX)`) and `SqlitePoller.subscribe`'s `this.caughtUpThrough.get(topic) ?? this.maxId(topic)`. Note the early-return guard at catchup.ts:434 also skips the LRU refresh, so a topic sitting at its tail (repeated empty catch-up pages, `rowid <= seen`) never refreshes and is evicted ahead of less-active topics — worth stating in the same doc fix.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none for part (1). Part (2)'s stderr line newly emits output on a run that today is silent, which a test asserting zero stderr writes during subscribe would notice.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: For part (2): `test/background-jobs.test.ts`'s 'a throwing handler is a consumer fault, not a store outage > ... keeps delivering, stays silent, stays live' asserts silence on stderr, and `test/lifecycle.test.ts` spies on stderr in places — none of them evict 1024 topics, so I expect no break, but I did not run part (2) since I did not implement it. Part (1) is a comment edit and breaks nothing.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If only the doc is corrected, the loss remains exactly as today — the finding is that the loss is undisclosed, not that the bound is wrong. If the stderr line is added without the doc fix, an operator gets a line whose meaning is documented nowhere.

summary: `SqliteStore -> SqliteCatchUp -> SqliteRetention -> SqlitePoller -> SqlitePlugin` is a five-level implementation-inheritance chain in which every intermediate class is `abstract`, has exactly one subclass, and is exported from no public entry point (`src/index.ts` exports only `SqlitePlugin` plus free functions). It buys nothing an ordinary module split would not — there is no second variant and no polymorphism — and it costs the thing this package is most sensitive to: each layer declares protected mutable state whose lifecycle is managed two or three layers away. `caughtUpThrough` is declared in catchup.ts, cleared in index.ts, read in poll.ts; `pruneTimer`/`pruneBatchTimer`/`pruneFailures`/`lastPruneDiag` are declared in retention.ts and created, reset and cleared in index.ts; `health`/`cancellers` are declared in poll.ts and reset in index.ts.
failure: Concrete consequence today: `connect()` resets `health`, `pruneFailures`, `lastPruneDiag`, `stopped`, `generation`, the driver, the store id and every prepared statement — but not `cancellers` and not `caughtUpThrough`, which only `disconnect()` clears. That is safe purely by accident of two other rules (a failed connect never reaches the assignments, and `connect()` refuses when already connected). Add a sixth per-connection field to any layer and both `connect()` and `disconnect()` must be edited from a different file than the one that declares it, with no compiler or test forcing either edit — which is exactly how the four ungraded prune-diagnostic resets in this review's second finding came to be invisible.
remediation: Do NOT flatten to one class with `#private` fields — see the breakage note below. The proportionate fix is to give each layer ownership of its own lifecycle: add `protected resetForConnect()` / `protected releaseForDisconnect()` to `SqliteStore` and override-and-super them in each layer, so `connect()`/`disconnect()` call one method each and a field added to `SqliteRetention` is reset in `SqliteRetention`. That keeps every field name and every test cast intact while removing the cross-file coupling. Making the chain a set of composed collaborators is the better end state but is a much larger change and should be weighed against the ratchet cost below.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'per-connection state a lifecycle method forgets to reset'. Add a behavioural (not structural) case: connect -> drive every entry point so every mutable field is dirtied (post, fetchRecent on several topics, subscribe, force a prune failure) -> disconnect -> connect -> assert the instance is indistinguishable from a freshly-constructed-and-connected one, by comparing `Object.entries(plugin)` field-by-field against a control instance rather than by naming fields. Written that way it grades the invariant from a place a rename or a move cannot invalidate, and it fails for a field added to any layer and reset in none — unlike `test/bounded-state.test.ts`, whose `perCall: ['cancellers','health']` grades field NAMES and therefore cements the current layout.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `SqlitePlugin.connect` (index.ts:52-72) and `disconnect` (index.ts:75-97) being the only writers of the reset fields, which I verified by grep across src/. The `resetForConnect` variant relies on the fact that `connect()`'s bump ordering is load-bearing (`this.generation++` must sit below every throw), so the hook has to be invoked at that exact point, not before validation and not before `openDriver`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — behaviour is unchanged by construction; only the location of the assignments moves.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: For the recommended per-layer-reset variant: none that I can find — the field names, their visibility and their values are unchanged, so `test/bounded-state.test.ts`'s `Object.entries(p)` walk and its `perCall: ['cancellers','health']` array still match, and the ~14 files that cast to `{ driver, pruneStmt, prune, storeId, caughtUpThrough }` still resolve. For the flatten-to-`#private` variant, which I am NOT recommending: `test/bounded-state.test.ts` breaks outright (`Object.entries` cannot see `#private` fields, so `expect(collections.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)` fails), as do every `as unknown as { driver: ... }` cast in test/background-jobs.test.ts, test/driver-parity.test.ts, test/conformance.test.ts, test/lifecycle.test.ts and test/subscription-health.test.ts. That is a large, real cost and I want it on the record rather than discovered mid-fix.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing observable is broken today, so applying this fixes no user-visible defect — it removes a class of future omission. If applied while the prune-diagnostic coverage gap remains open, a reset moved into the wrong layer would still ship green, so this should land after or with that finding's test, not instead of it.

summary: The 'better-sqlite3 is absent' fake — a ~25-line `vi.doMock('node:module')` that wraps `createRequire` to throw MODULE_NOT_FOUND for a named id — is restated in four files: src/driver.test.ts, test/at-rest-mode.test.ts, test/conformance.test.ts (`loadFallbackPlugin`) and test/driver-parity.test.ts (`loadWithout`). The copies have already drifted: only driver-parity's distinguishes `ERR_UNKNOWN_BUILTIN_MODULE` for `node:` ids, and only conformance's re-checks the resolved `driver.kind` afterwards. The comments cross-reference each other ('driver-parity.test.ts uses the same trick for its narrower cases'), which is the tell. Separately, 16 of the 20 test files each mint their own `mkdtempSync` scratch-database helper (6 under the name `dbFile`) and 14 restate an `open[]` array plus an `afterEach` that disconnects it — the whole package's teardown discipline is copy-pasted, and a leak fixed in one file is not fixed in the others.
failure: A human reviewing this suite must read the same fake four times to learn whether the fallback is being simulated the same way each time, and cannot tell from any one of them that a fifth caller would get the weaker two-code version. Concretely: the copy in test/at-rest-mode.test.ts throws plain MODULE_NOT_FOUND for every id, so if a case there ever hid a `node:` builtin it would exercise `versionHint`'s MODULE_NOT_FOUND arm instead of its ERR_UNKNOWN_BUILTIN_MODULE arm and grade the wrong branch — a divergence invisible from that file.
remediation: Extract one `test/absent-modules.ts` exporting `loadWithout(missing: string[])` returning `{ openDriver, SqlitePlugin }` (driver-parity's version is the strictest and is the right base), and have all four call it. `vi.doMock` is not hoisted, so calling it from a helper module is safe — that is why the existing call sites already wrap it in an async function. Extract a second `test/scratch-store.ts` exporting the temp-dir/db-path helper and a `tracked()`/`afterEach` teardown pair. The package already ships `test/health.ts` as a shared helper, so the precedent and the tsconfig.test.json coverage are in place.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a fixture restated per file, drifting between copies'. This one is a merge rather than an addition, so the durable ratchet is a lint-style case over `test/**` and `src/**/*.test.ts`: assert that no more than one file contains a `doMock('node:module')` call, and that the number of distinct `mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), ...))` call sites is at most the number of files exporting a shared fixture. Written as a glob over the test tree (not a list of file paths) it survives files being added, renamed or moved, and it is the invariant — one definition per fixture — rather than the current layout.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The distinction between `vi.mock` (hoisted to the top of the importing file, so it cannot live in a helper) and `vi.doMock` (not hoisted). All four current call sites use `doMock` inside an `async function`, which is what makes extraction possible; I read all four to confirm.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: For the extracted helper: the at-rest-mode copy's behaviour changes — it would begin throwing ERR_UNKNOWN_BUILTIN_MODULE for `node:` ids where it currently throws MODULE_NOT_FOUND. That is the stricter behaviour, but it is a behaviour change to a fixture and must be checked case by case, not assumed inert.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found, but this is the weakest claim in my report: I did not perform the extraction and did not run it. The risk I can name concretely is `vi.resetModules()`/`vi.doUnmock` ordering — conformance.test.ts unmocks in its `cleanup`, driver-parity.test.ts in an `afterEach`, and a shared helper that owns neither could leave a mock live across files if vitest is run with a shared environment.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken today; the drift I found (the ERR_UNKNOWN_BUILTIN_MODULE arm) is latent, not active, because no current at-rest-mode case hides a `node:` builtin. Merging removes the ability for a fifth copy to grade the wrong branch silently.

summary: `subscriptionHealth()` returns `this.health.map((h) => ({ ...h }))`. Replacing that with `this.health.slice()` leaves the suite 766/766 green, so nothing grades the snapshot contract of the one programmatic surface this plugin adds beyond the seam. The README sells it as the embedder's health-check path ('an embedder ... can read that state programmatically') and asserts a temporal property about it ('After disconnect() every topic reads stopped rather than keeping its last live state'), which is only meaningful if a report taken before disconnect and a report taken after are distinct objects.
failure: With `.slice()`: an embedder does `const before = plugin.subscriptionHealth()`, later calls `await plugin.disconnect()`, then logs `before` — and reads `state: 'stopped', lastError: 'disconnected'` for a snapshot taken while the loop was live, because `disconnect()` (index.ts:86-89) mutates the very records it handed out. Worse in the other direction: the embedder can write `plugin.subscriptionHealth()[0].consecutiveFailures = 0` and corrupt the plugin's own bookkeeping, since the poll tick reads and writes those same objects. Neither turns a test red today.
remediation: No product change needed — add the assertions. In `test/subscription-health.test.ts`: capture a report while a loop is live, tear the plugin down, and assert the captured report is unchanged; and mutate a field of a returned record, then assert the next `subscriptionHealth()` call is unaffected.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a public accessor that leaks live internal state'. Rather than one hand-written pair, parameterize over every array-or-object-returning public method of `SqlitePlugin` (today `subscriptionHealth()` and `fetchRecent().messages`): for each, take a report, deep-freeze a structural clone of it, drive the plugin through a state change (a post, a failing tick, a disconnect), and assert the original report deep-equals the clone; then mutate the returned value and assert the next call is unaffected. Enumerating the methods from the prototype rather than listing them means a future accessor is graded the day it is added.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `SqlitePlugin.disconnect` (index.ts:86-89) mutating `h.state` and `h.lastError` in place on the records `this.health` holds, and the poll tick's closure holding the same `health` object it pushed at poll.ts:522. Both traced.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Any future `subscriptionHealth()` that returns the live records, or a shallow copy that shares a nested mutable value if the record ever grows one.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. `test/health.ts`'s `expectHealth` compares by value (`toEqual` on mapped discriminants), so it is indifferent to identity and will not conflict. `test/lifecycle.test.ts`'s 'every live loop reads as stopped after disconnect, and stays that way' reads a report AFTER disconnect, which is the case that already passes either way — it is the before/after pair that is missing.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken today; the shipped code copies correctly. This removes the ability to regress it silently. If it were added while the copy were already gone, it would go red immediately, which is the test I want.

summary: CLAUDE.md is explicit: a comment earns its place only by warning a future developer off a risky action, phrased as 'keep X, so that Y'; 'why an approach was chosen over another, what a reviewer suggested and why it was declined' belongs in the commit message. A large share of this package's comments are the excluded kind. src/driver.ts:174-180 justifies why the module load is split from the DB open; src/driver.ts:255 explains why a constructor sits outside a try/catch; src/config.ts carries paragraph-length rationale on nearly every exported constant. The test tree is worse: test/bounded-state.test.ts:96 ('Both arms are pinned, so replacing the eviction with a `clear()` (which satisfies the bound above perfectly) reds here') and test/conformance.test.ts:38-46 ('So the driver is a DIMENSION of this file rather than an ambient fact') are written to a reviewer, not to a maintainer.
failure: The failure mode is rot rather than a wrong output: src/poll.ts:512's justification is already false against test/bounded-state.test.ts (see the eviction finding above) and nothing noticed, because a comment that argues cannot be checked while a comment that warns usually can. The density also crowds out the ones that matter — driver.ts:205-208's genuine 'keep this ahead of the driver open, so that there is no window in which the store is world-readable' is buried among five neighbours that merely narrate.
remediation: Sweep the package against the CLAUDE.md rule. Keep every 'keep X, so that Y' warning. Move the justifications (why the loader is split, why the constructor is outside the try, why each bound was chosen) into the commit that introduced them. Where a comment exists because the code is hard to read — driver.ts's `storeFiles` is the clearest case, needing eight lines to explain a two-branch function — file against the code: name it for what it answers and let the signature carry the rest. Delete reviewer-addressed prose from tests outright; a test name is where that argument belongs.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'comments that argue rather than warn'. `packages/bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts` already exists and is the right home: extend it with a glob over every package's `src/**` and `test/**` that flags block comments over N lines which contain none of the sanctioned warning forms ('keep ... so that', 'never', 'do not'), with an explicit, reviewed allowlist of file+first-line pairs rather than a count — so the allowlist is the record of what was adjudicated and shrinking it is visible in a diff. A count-based ratchet would let a new essay in as an old one is deleted.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: CLAUDE.md's 'Comments are a last resort' section as the stated rule, and the existing packages/bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts as the established place this repo enforces source conventions from. I read the latter's presence but not its full body, so whether it is the right host is an assumption.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A new multi-line justification comment in any package, unless allowlisted — which is a real friction cost on every future contributor and the main reason to weigh this against its value.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none from the comment deletions themselves. But `test/readme-claims.test.ts` and `packages/bridge-core/src/readme-truth.test.ts` grade prose by regex, and I did NOT audit whether any of them matches text inside a source comment rather than a README — if one does, deleting that comment reds it. That check is the first thing to do before touching anything.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing functional. This is the lowest-yield item in my report and I am filing it because the rule is stated and mechanically checkable, not because it is where the risk is — it should not be allowed to displace the ordering-key or prune-diagnostic work.

summary: The whole 1871-test suite stays green when a macrotask gap is opened between `waiter.cancel()` and `waiter = this.armWaiter(room)` in `blockingMam`. long-poll-wake.test.ts declares the invariant "from the moment a blocking fetch starts until it returns, the room's waiter set is never empty" and every one of its 32 cells samples `waiters.size` at delivery — but delivery is only ever triggered inside the join, inside a MAM round trip, or during a park, never at the re-arm. The source comment ("Re-arm with no await in between, so that the room's set is never empty while this call is still running and a reflection cannot slip through the gap") is un-ratcheted: it is the one window of the blocking path nothing grades.
failure: Mutate archive.ts:181-182 to `waiter.cancel(); await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0)); waiter = this.armWaiter(room);` — the exact defect the comment forbids — and `npx vitest run packages/bridge-xmpp` reports `Test Files 36 passed, Tests 1871 passed`. A live reflection landing in that gap fires into an empty set and is lost; the caller then waits out the current lag-poll step (50 ms doubling per timeout, unbounded up to the remaining budget) on a message the archive already holds.
remediation: Grade the declared invariant instead of sampling it at three chosen instants: install a watcher over the room's waiter registration for the lifetime of a blocking fetch and assert it never observes the set empty. Concretely, add a `withWaiterWatch(plugin, room)` helper next to `expectNoLeaks` in test/fake-xmpp.ts that swaps `priv(plugin).waiters` for a Map subclass recording every transition to "no set, or an empty set, for this room" between the fetch starting and resolving, and assert the recording is empty. Apply it to all existing wakeCells rather than adding a 33rd cell.
testUpgrade: Class = "a wake source re-armed across an await, anywhere on the blocking path". Parameterize the ARRIVAL axis of long-poll-wake.test.ts by WINDOW OF THE PATH and add the two windows it is missing — 'in the re-arm between two polls' and 'between the park resolving and the next read' — driven off the waiter-registration watcher above rather than off fixture hooks, so a window added by a future refactor is covered by the invariant instead of needing its own cell. The existing `wakeCells` table is too narrow because every arrival it names is triggered by a hook the fixture owns (`onDiscoRequest`, `onMamRequest`, `onMamInFlight`, a timer), and no hook exists at the re-arm.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `XmppArchive.armWaiter` reading and writing `this.waiters` on every call (`const set = this.waiters.get(room) ?? new Set(); this.waiters.set(room, set); set.add(fire);`) and `fire` deleting the room key when the set empties (`if (set?.size === 0) this.waiters.delete(room)`) — the watcher depends on that delete branch, since that is the transition it must observe. Also on the existing `priv()` cast in test/fake-xmpp.ts, which already exposes `waiters: Map<string, Set<(reason: string) => void>>`.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — it is a test-only addition; no production input changes.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at runtime. In the suite it newly rejects any implementation that lets the room's waiter registration go empty while a blocking fetch is outstanding, including a legitimate future refactor that de-registers before re-registering.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I ran the full package suite unmutated (36 files / 1871 tests green) and then with the gap mutation (still green), so nothing today depends on the set being allowed to empty mid-call. I looked in long-poll-wake.test.ts, long-poll-query-budget.test.ts and pending-registry.test.ts ('waiters: one long-poll timing out leaves a concurrent long-poll on the same room armed'), which is the only other test that reads `waiters`.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken in shipped behaviour today — the re-arm is genuinely synchronous. If the guard is added and someone later reintroduces the gap, the guard catches it; if the guard is NOT added, the gap can be reintroduced silently by any refactor that puts an await between the cancel and the arm.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The orderings that matter: (a) stanza handler runs in macrotask M1 while the fetch's continuation is a microtask of M0 — today no gap, so the reflection always finds a registered waiter; (b) with the gap, M1 falls between cancel and arm and the wake is dropped; (c) two blocking fetches on the same room — the second's waiter is a separate entry in the same Set, so the watcher must key on "this fetch's own registration" or on "the room key present with size > 0", and I chose the latter, which is correct for two callers because either caller's registration keeps the key non-empty and neither can be starved by the other's cancel.

summary: `archivedItem` reads `archId: result.attrs.id ?? ''`, so a MAM `<result>` carrying no `id` (or an empty one) becomes an archive row whose cursor is the empty string. `fetchRecent` then hands `''` back as `nextCursor` — and `mamQueryIq` deliberately treats `after === ''` as "omit `<after/>` entirely", i.e. "this room's archive from message one". The cursor moves BACKWARDS, past everything the caller has already read, and stays there: every subsequent catch-up re-reads the whole archive and lands on `''` again. XEP-0313 makes `id` mandatory on `<result>`, so the correct answer is to refuse the row, not to coin a zero cursor from it. Reachable a second way: `limit <= 0` makes `lastPageMam` read nothing, leaving `tail` undefined and `nextCursor` `''` for a since-less call.
failure: Archive two rows in a room, blank the second row's `id` on the wire (a `<result>` with no `id` attribute), then `fetchRecent({ topic, since: <first row's real archive id>, limit: 10 })`. Reproduced: `messages = ['two']`, `nextCursor = ""`. Feeding that cursor back replays the entire room from message one, forever. Second reproduction: `fetchRecent({ topic, limit: 0 })` over a non-empty archive -> `messages = []`, `nextCursor = ""`.
remediation: In `archivedItem`, return `undefined` when `result.attrs.id` is absent or empty — a row with no archive position is not a row this seam can carry, exactly as a row with no `<message>` is not. Additionally floor the cursor in `fetchRecent`: when the computed `nextCursor` would be `''` and `args.since` was a non-empty string, return `args.since` — a read must never hand back a position behind the one it was given.
testUpgrade: Class = "fetchRecent returns a nextCursor that is not strictly at-or-after the one it was given". Add a property/table case to archive-admission.test.ts's existing `cursorRows` cross that fuzzes the ARCHIVE ROW ITSELF, not just its body: rows with `id` absent, `id=''`, `id` equal to the caller's `since`, and `id` repeated from an earlier row — crossed with the three `since` arms already there — and assert in every cell that `String(nextCursor) !== ''` unless `since` was itself `''`, and that replaying `nextCursor` returns nothing already returned. Widen the same generator over `limit` in {0, 1, 2, 100}. The existing cursorRows table cannot catch this because FakeXmpp.archiveItem always mints `arch-${++seq}`, so no cell can produce a blank archive id, and the tool boundary's `z.number().positive()` means no cell ever passes limit 0.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `XmppArchive.exclusiveMam`'s `const pageTail = page.items.at(-1)?.archId; if (pageTail !== undefined) tail = pageTail;` and its strict-advance branch `if (pageTail === cursor) throw`, plus `lastPageMam`'s `const head = page.items[0]?.archId; if (page.complete || head === undefined) break;`. Dropping an id-less row from `page.items` shifts both to the last/first row that DOES carry an id; `complete` still comes from the server's `<fin>`, so neither loop can spin. Also relies on `wire.mamQueryIq`'s existing `if (opts.after !== undefined && opts.after !== '')` guard staying as-is.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A MAM `<result>` with no `id` attribute (or `id=''`) is now silently dropped from the page instead of carried as a message with `backendMsgId: ''`. If such a row also carried a `<body>`, that message is no longer delivered on the catch-up path — it was already undeliverable in any useful sense, since core would store `''` as its dedup key and its cursor.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I looked at archive-admission.test.ts (both describes), cursor-inputs.test.ts, empty-archive-catchup.test.ts, mam-paging.test.ts and mam-provenance.test.ts: every one of them builds rows through `FakeXmpp.archiveItem`/`feedMamResult`, which always sets `id: item.archId = 'arch-N'`, so no existing assertion observes an id-less result. The `nextCursor` floor in fetchRecent is a no-op for every case in the empty-archive/zero-cursor tables, since those pass `since` as `''` or omit it.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If only the `fetchRecent` floor is applied and `archivedItem` still coins `''`, the rewind is hidden for a since-carrying read but the row is still delivered to core with `backendMsgId: ''` — a dedup key that collides with every other id-less row in every room. That is why the `archivedItem` guard is the primary fix and the floor is the belt.

summary: `fetchRecent` arms its waiter, then returns immediately if `roomExists` is false — and `roomExists` answers false not only for a room that is genuinely absent but for every inconclusive probe (`service-unavailable`, `remote-server-timeout`, an IQ that never comes back), by design. So `blockMs` is silently dropped on exactly those inputs, while `test/conformance.test.ts` declares `supportsBlockingFetch: true`. The conformance suite's own words for this shape are "native-block-actually-waits: a plugin declaring native blockMs support gave up on the budget at once, which makes core long-poll it in a hot loop" — it just never exercises it, because every conformance case posts first. This is not a hang, since core's `fetchRecentBlocking` falls back to its generic poll, but it is a behaviour a reasonable operator would not predict: a 60 s long-poll on a not-yet-created topic issues ~240 disco#info IQs at the default `block_poll_interval_ms` of 250 instead of one native park, and the README's long-poll paragraph promises unconditionally that "the call holds up to block_ms for a new message before returning".
failure: With `FakeXmpp.discoUnknownRoom = 'item-not-found'` (or `discoProbe = 'no-answer'`), `await plugin.fetchRecent({ topic: asTopic('t-absent'), since: asCursor('x1'), blockMs: 2000 })` returns in 1 ms with `{messages: [], nextCursor: 'x1'}`. Expected under the declared native-blocking capability: a return no earlier than ~2000 ms, or a documented and asserted exception.
remediation: Decide it and state it. Either (a) hoist the existence probe inside the blocking loop so a `blockMs` fetch re-probes on a bounded cadence until the room appears or the budget expires — note this cannot use the waiter, since a room this connection is not in routes it nothing, so it must poll; or (b) keep the early return, add the exception to the README's `block_ms` paragraph ("a topic whose MUC room does not yet exist, or whose existence probe cannot be answered, returns at once; core's generic long-poll covers the wait"), and assert the elapsed time in the long-poll cell that already exists in read-path-creation.test.ts so the behaviour is chosen rather than incidental.
testUpgrade: Class = "a plugin declaring supportsBlockingFetch returns before its budget for some input class". read-path-creation.test.ts already has the discriminating row — `{ name: 'fetchRecent long-polling', run: (plugin, topic) => plugin.fetchRecent({ topic, since: asCursor(''), blockMs: 400 }) }` crossed with 5 probe answers and 2 existence values — but grades only the creation handshake, never elapsed time. Add an elapsed-time expectation to that cell parameterized over the probe axis, so every way the probe can fail to answer is graded for the block contract and not just for provisioning. In packages/conformance, widen cases/blocking.ts with a since-less blocking read on a topic that has NEVER been posted to, so the class is graded once for every backend rather than per-plugin.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: For (a): `XmppRooms.roomExists`'s early exit `if (this.joined.has(room)) return true;` and its rule that only `<iq type='result'>` is evidence — a polling loop must keep that, so that a room this connection could not confirm is still never joined. For (b): `XmppPlugin.fetchRecent`'s `finally { waiter?.cancel(); }`, which already means the early return leaks nothing.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: Option (a) newly accepts a `blockMs` fetch on an absent topic as a call that parks for the budget — i.e. the tool call now holds for up to `catchup.block_max_ms` where it used to return immediately.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none for (b). For (a), nothing is rejected, but a caller that relied on an absent topic answering instantly now waits.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: For (a): read-path-creation.test.ts's 'fetchRecent long-polling' cells would each go from ~milliseconds to 400 ms (10 cells x 400 ms), and 'XMPP reads an absent topic as an empty, replayable page' passes no blockMs so is unaffected. I did not find a case that asserts an absent-topic blocking read returns fast, so none would go red — only slower. For (b): no test changes behaviour; the new elapsed assertion must be watched failing against today's code first (it does: 1 ms observed).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If (b) is applied alone, the IQ amplification during a MUC hiccup remains — an operator whose MUC answers `service-unavailable` still pays 240 probes per long-poll per topic. (b) makes it a known cost rather than a surprise; only (a) removes it.
remediationCheck.interleavings: For (a): the poll loop must re-check `this.stopped` each round exactly as `blockingMam` does, or a disconnect mid-poll leaves a probe loop running against a stopped client; and two concurrent blocking fetches on the same absent topic each run their own probe loop, which is the same duplication `roomExists` already tolerates today.

summary: `roomStanzaId`'s JSDoc says: "Keep the `by` filter, so that a `<stanza-id>` an occupant put on its own message — which the MUC reflects verbatim — is never read as a position in the archive." Both halves cannot be true at once. The filter accepts precisely `by === room`, which is the value a hostile occupant would write; if the MUC really did reflect it verbatim, the filter would admit the forgery. The protection actually comes from XEP-0359 §5 — a routing entity strips a `<stanza-id>` attributed to itself — and the fixture encodes exactly that in `FakeXmpp.reflectable()` ("a live Prosody does exactly that for `<stanza-id by='room'>`"). The doc credits the code for a guarantee the SERVER provides, which is the shape that makes a future reader delete the server dependency from their threat model.
failure: Read the claim, then the code: `stanza.getChildren('stanza-id', NS_SID).find((e) => e.attrs.by === room)?.attrs.id`. Feed the live path a `<message type='groupchat' from='room@svc/eve'>` carrying an occupant-authored `<stanza-id xmlns='urn:xmpp:sid:0' by='room@svc' id='forged'/>` — which is what the doc asserts a MUC delivers — and `roomStanzaId` returns `'forged'`, which becomes the message's `cursor` and `backendMsgId`. The filter stops `by='eve@svc'` and `by` absent; it does not stop the case the sentence names.
remediation: Reword to name the real mechanism and the real dependency, e.g. "Read only the `<stanza-id>` this ROOM attributed to itself. A co-occupant's own `<stanza-id>` is stripped by the MUC (XEP-0359 §5) before this connection sees it; the `by` filter is what stops one attributed to any OTHER entity from being read as a position in this room's archive." Leave `reflectable()`'s comment as the statement of the server dependency, since that is where it is enforced.
testUpgrade: Class = "a comment or JSDoc that credits local code for a guarantee an upstream component provides". live-field-provenance.test.ts already crosses `by` over {this room, another occupant, a stranger, the MUC service component, absent} and pins the four the filter rejects — extend the same table with a row for `by = the room itself, injected by an occupant` whose EXPECTATION is that `FakeXmpp.reflectable()` never delivers it, so the test names the stripping server as the thing under test rather than the filter. That makes the dependency a graded fixture contract instead of a sentence.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `FakeXmpp.reflectable()`'s branch `return attrs.by !== room && attrs.from !== room;`, which is the fixture's encoding of the server-side strip and is what the new table row would assert against.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. comment-discipline.test.ts only lints `//` line comments, not JSDoc blocks (its own header says so), so a JSDoc rewrite cannot trip it. I checked live-field-provenance.test.ts and mam-provenance.test.ts for an assertion on this sentence's wording; there is none.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Rewording alone changes no behaviour: if a deployment runs a MUC that does not strip (a non-conformant or old component), a co-occupant can still choose this connection's cursor and dedup key for a message. The honest doc makes that dependency visible; only a server requirement in the README (alongside the existing MAM requirement) would let an operator act on it.

summary: The gate that exists because review filed "a comment that restates the code" twice is a keyword sniff: `RISK = /\b(?:so that|so a|so it|keep|never|cannot|can't|would|rather than|or an?\b|otherwise)\b/i`. Four of those alternatives — `keep`, `never`, `cannot`, `would` — are words a restatement uses as freely as a warning, and `keep` is the first word of the very phrasing CLAUDE.md prescribes, so any restatement written in the house style passes. The it.each matcher table underneath it is what makes the run look non-vacuous, but every `false` fixture in it happens to avoid all ten alternatives, so the table cannot expose the hole. src/rooms.ts:280 is already through it today: "// If the join fails, drop the cache so a later call can retry" is a restatement of `p.catch(() => { if (this.joined.get(room) === p) this.forgetRoom(room); })`.
failure: Insert `// Keep the index of the slash.` above `resourceOf` in src/jid.ts — a pure restatement of `const i = full.indexOf('/');` — and `npx vitest run packages/bridge-xmpp/test/comment-discipline.test.ts` reports `Test Files 1 passed`. The offenders list stays empty because the comment contains the word "keep".
remediation: Require a CONSEQUENCE connective rather than an imperative verb: `/(so that|so a\b|so it\b|otherwise|rather than|because|\bor an?\b|would)/i`. Measured against the current sources: this rejects the planted restatement, and every existing `//` comment in src/ still passes (jid.ts:26 via "because", rooms.ts:327 via "would"). It does not yet catch rooms.ts:280, which uses "so a" for a restatement — so pair the regex change with deleting that comment, since a lint that cannot be satisfied by the code it is pointed at is the wrong lint.
testUpgrade: Class = "a mechanical gate whose matcher is graded only by fixtures the matcher was written from". Make the matcher table ADVERSARIAL rather than illustrative: add rows that pair each admitted connective with an obvious restatement (`['Keep the index of the slash.', false]`, `['This would return the resource.', false]`, `['Never mind the empty case.', false]`, `['Or a colon, or a slash.', false]`) alongside the current true rows, so a widening of RISK that lets a restatement through fails the table itself. Then assert the coupling the suite is missing: that the matcher table and the source scan use the SAME regex object (they do today, but nothing pins it), so narrowing one cannot silently leave the other.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `lineComments()`'s run-joining behaviour (`open.text = ${open.text} ${text}`), so a consequence stated on the last line of a run still satisfies the narrowed regex — I re-ran the joiner over all of src/ with the narrowed pattern to get the two-comment result above, so this is measured, not assumed.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — the narrowed regex is a strict subset of the current one for the alternatives it keeps, plus `because`, which today's regex does not admit at all. So it newly accepts a comment that states a reason with `because` and nothing else.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Any `//` comment in src/ whose only qualifying word is a bare `keep`, `never`, `cannot`/`can't`, or `rather than` with no consequence clause. Measured over the current tree: zero existing comments, since jid.ts:26 carries `because` and rooms.ts:327 carries `would`.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I ran the narrowed pattern over every `//` comment in packages/bridge-xmpp/src and got an empty offender list, which is the only assertion the `no comment restates the code` case makes. The it.each matcher rows would all still grade the same way: the four `true` fixtures carry `so that`/`or an`/`rather than`/`would`, and the five `false` fixtures carry none of the narrowed alternatives. bridge-core's repo-wide source-hygiene.test.ts is a separate lint and is not this package's to edit.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Narrowing the regex without deleting rooms.ts:280 leaves that restatement green (it says "so a"), so the gate still certifies at least one instance of the class it was written for. The regex change alone is therefore an improvement, not a closure.

summary: `wakeCells` crosses 4 arrivals x 4 archival lags (0/50/400/1000 ms) x 2 MAM latencies (0/200 ms) = 32 cells, and it is the dominant cost of the package suite (~30 s of ~104 s of test time; several cells are individually 1.3-2.0 s). Under the mutation the file's header exists to catch — arming the waiter after `roomExists`+`ensureJoinedRoom` instead of before the first await — exactly the 8 cells of the `inside the join` arrival fail, all eight identically, and none of the other 24 fires. The lag and latency axes therefore carry no discriminating power for the invariant the arrival axis grades: 8 near-copies that can only fail together, priced at ~64 s under failure and ~7 s green.
failure: Apply the mutation to src/index.ts:202 (`const waiter = blockMs > 0 ? this.armWaiter(room) : undefined;` moved below `await this.ensureJoinedRoom(room)`) and run the file: 8 failures, every one of them `a live copy arriving 'inside the join' ..., {0|50|400|1000} ms archival lag, {0|200} ms round trip`, each timing out at ~8000 ms. The other 24 cells pass. No pair of the 8 can fail independently of the others.
remediation: Keep the arrival axis at full width — it is the one that discriminates — and collapse the lag x latency cross to the two values that change the code path rather than the four x two that change only the clock: lag in {0, 400} (0 exercises the no-lag arm, 400 exercises the doubling ladder past its first step) and latency in {0, 200}. That is 4 x 2 x 2 = 16 cells.
