summary: `commentLines` only recognises a comment when the TRIMMED line starts with `//` or `/*`, so every trailing comment on a line of code is invisible to the lint. Ten such comments exist in src/ today (push-loop.ts:126,130,136,203,209,211 and history.ts:75,85,191,192), several of which restate the line they annotate — `lastEventId = ev.id; // ack heartbeats too`, `needsGapFillFrom = undefined; // gap closed — resume normal polling`, `return true; // re-check liveness / re-attempt before polling the fresh queue`, `cursor = last.cursor; // advance so a retry resumes past this delivered page` — which is the shape CLAUDE.md bans. The lint's only control asserts `files.length > 0`, never that the extractor sees a comment.
failure: Add `export const REVIEWER_NOTE = 1; // as discussed with the reviewer, we chose this instead; it is perfectly safe` to src/wire.ts. That single line trips three of the three BANNED patterns ('as discussed', 'we chose', 'perfectly safe') and the run stays green: comment-hygiene.test.ts reports 42 passed / 42.
remediation: Extend `commentLines` to also emit the tail of a code line from an unquoted `//`. Do it by stripping string and template literals from the line FIRST and then taking the tail from the last surviving `//`; a naive `indexOf('//')` misfires on `DEFAULT_SITE_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:9991'` in src/config.ts and would report `/127.0.0.1:9991'` as a comment. Then add a positive control alongside 'finds the package source to lint': assert the extractor returns a known trailing comment (e.g. that some entry's text contains 'ack heartbeats too'), so a future refactor cannot silently blind it again. Landing the extractor will surface the ten existing trailing comments — file against the CODE per CLAUDE.md (name `acked` so the ack is obvious, hoist the dedup condition into a named predicate) rather than merely deleting the words.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'a source lint whose extractor silently sees less than the whole file'. Give every extractor-based lint in this package a POSITIVE control driven through the same function the lint uses — the pattern export-surface.test.ts already sets with 'reads every export shape it claims to grade' and config.test.ts with 'derives suffixes the validator cannot see'. Parameterize the control over comment placements: own-line `//`, own-line `/* */`, multi-line block, trailing `//` after code, trailing `/* */` after code, and `//` inside a string literal (which must NOT be reported) — a table that fails on the day the extractor stops seeing any placement.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The lint's own `BANNED` regex list and `MAX_SHARED_RUN` README-overlap check, both of which run unchanged over the newly-visible text. Depends on src/config.ts:26 `const DEFAULT_SITE_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:9991';` being the case the string-stripping must survive — I checked src/ for other `//` inside literals and this is the one.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a trailing comment carrying banned prose, and a trailing comment duplicating a 12-word run from the README.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: comment-hygiene.test.ts's own README-duplication case is the risk: widening the corpus adds ten comment texts to the normalized word stream, and `runs()` builds 12-word windows ACROSS the joined comments, so a window can straddle two previously-separate comments. I did not run the widened extractor, so I cannot say whether any straddle collides with the README — treat that as the thing to check first. No other test reads `commentLines`.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken at runtime; this restores a measurement. If applied without also fixing the code the newly-visible comments annotate, the lint will fail on those ten lines — which is the intended outcome, not a regression.

summary: The comment on the shared-bot deployment reads 'One entry, carrying the union of both sessions' reach — the merged phantom peer'. 'Entry' and 'reach' are roster vocabulary, and the roster does not merge: bridge-core/src/engine/presence.ts:85 `emitterOf` returns `asHandle(rec.handle)` whenever the beat's own payload carries a handle, falling back to `m.senderHandle` only for a pre-field beat. The zulip README (lines 155-160) states this correctly — 'sessions sharing one bot still appear as separate peers, each under its configured identity.handle'. The test file whose stated purpose is 'so the prose and the wire cannot drift' therefore carries a comment asserting the drift it exists to prevent, and nothing in this package grades the roster claim the README makes.
failure: Read packages/bridge-zulip/test/presence-attribution.test.ts:24 next to packages/bridge-zulip/README.md:155-160 and packages/bridge-core/src/engine/presence.ts:85. Rather than one more assertion, give the claim a locator: have this file's assertion import the symbol the claim depends on (`emitterOf`'s behaviour via core's public presence surface) so a change to core's handle precedence breaks a zulip test by NAME, and parameterize the deployments table with the roster-key expectation alongside the sender expectation so the two never again describe different worlds. The same table shape should cover a beat with no `handle` field (the compatibility fallback), which is the only case where the comment's 'merged phantom peer' would actually be true — today no row distinguishes the two.

If a future core change made the fallback lead, the README paragraph becomes the wrong one and the comment the right one.

summary: `subscribe()` is the only seam call with no `generation` capture. `post`/`fetchRecent` both capture `this.generation` before their first await and refuse to act on a retired session; `subscribe` resolves `channelId`, writes `this.subs`, then awaits `gateway.ensureUp()` and `GET /channels/<id>` with no such guard. A `connect()` landing in either window runs `forgetTopics()` -> `subs.clear()`, and `subscribe` then returns SUCCESS with the subscription gone and nothing on stderr. The package's own `session-lifetime.test.ts` declares this class ("a seam call that resumes into the session that REPLACED the one it was made in") but its PARKS table holds only three `fetchRecent` rows.
failure: connect({channel_map:{chat:'111'}}); subscribe(asTopic('chat'), h) parks on `GET /channels/111`; connect({channel_map:{chat:'111'}}) again; release the check -> `await plugin.subscribe(...)` RESOLVES undefined while `probe(plugin,'subs').has('111') === false`. Core's push-loop reads a resolved subscribe as "live push wired" and never retries, so that topic is permanently deaf to MESSAGE_CREATE with no diagnostic. Reproduced under fake timers. Sharper arm, traced not reproduced: `channelId` is captured pre-await, so if the new config maps the topic elsewhere, `unpushableReason` validates the OLD id under the NEW session and a `10003` there throws NoSuchTopicError out of subscribe — core then skips a topic that is perfectly valid in the successor session.
remediation: Capture `const generation = this.generation;` as the first statement of `subscribe()` (alongside `this.require()`), and after EACH await check `if (generation !== this.generation) { warn(`live push for topic ${named} was not wired: its session was retired mid-subscribe`); return; }` before touching `this.subs` again. Make the two `this.subs.delete(channelId)` error paths conditional on the same check so a retired call cannot delete the successor's entry. `unpushableReason` should be given the captured generation too, or re-resolve `channelId` after the ensureUp await.
testUpgrade: Widen `session-lifetime.test.ts`'s PARKS table from a fetchRecent-only list to a table over EVERY seam call that awaits — post (parked on POST /messages), subscribe (parked on ensureUp AND parked on GET /channels/<id>), resolveIdentity (parked on GET /users/@me) — crossed with the existing RETIREMENTS axis. Each row asserts (a) the call does not query the successor session's channel, (b) nothing from the successor crosses under the old topic, and (c) for subscribe specifically, that a RESOLVED subscribe implies `probe(plugin,'subs').has(channelId)`, so "resolved but unwired" cannot pass. That last assertion is the class-level invariant and would also catch a future seam call added without a capture.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `this.generation` (session.ts:35, `protected generation = 0`, incremented in `connect()` before `forgetTopics()`), `warn()` from diagnostics.ts, and `forgetTopics()`'s `this.subs.clear()` (session.ts:81) which is what actually erases the entry.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at the seam — but a subscribe retired mid-flight now writes one line to stderr where today it is silent, and returns without a subscription instead of returning with a silently absent one.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I checked the two suites that assert stderr is EMPTY on a subscribe path — rest-contract.test.ts:1066 (`expect(written, 'a pushable channel was reported as unusable').toBe('')`) and the pushable rows of the channel-type table — neither retires the session mid-call, so the new warn cannot fire in them. session-lifetime.test.ts contains no subscribe row at all.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the bug remained (e.g. only the post-ensureUp check added, not the post-channel-check one), the second window still loses the subscription silently. It also does NOT fix the sharper arm on its own: the stale `channelId` still reaches `unpushableReason` unless the generation check is placed BEFORE that call, so a retired subscribe could still convert into a NoSuchTopicError rejection that fails core's attach.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Three orderings covered: (1) connect() lands while parked on ensureUp — check fires before subs is touched; (2) connect() lands while parked on GET /channels/<id> — check fires before the delete/warn branches; (3) two callers subscribing the same topic concurrently across one connect() — both capture the same pre-connect generation, both bail, and neither deletes the successor's entry, which is why the deletes must also be guarded. connect() itself has no awaits, so it is atomic with respect to these continuations.

summary: `allowed_mentions` — the mention BLAST-RADIUS knob, and the only `backend_config` key whose stated purpose is security ("`post` content can be untrusted inbound text an agent relayed") — is the one key whose value is not checked. `SHAPE_REFUSALS['nested object']` is `() => undefined`; `assertKnownConfigKeys` validates the container is an object and that member NAMES are declared, but never member TYPES. The object is then spliced verbatim into every `POST /channels/<id>/messages` body (index.ts:78).
failure: `connect({ token: 't', allowed_mentions: { parse: 'everyone' } })` RESOLVES (reproduced), as does `connect({ token: 't', allowed_mentions: { replied_user: 'yes', users: 5 } })`, while `connect({ token: 5 })` is correctly refused. Every subsequent `post` then ships that body to Discord and gets `400 Invalid Form Body (50035)`. The operator gets a bridge that loads clean, reports success, and cannot post a single message — the exact symptom README ¶82 says this validation exists to prevent ("a bridge that comes up reporting success and is wired to nothing"). README line 75's "Every key **and value** is checked before anything is dialled" is false for this key.
remediation: Replace the `'nested object'` ConfigShape (allowed_mentions is its only user) with a `'mention scope'` shape whose refusal checks: `parse` is an array whose every element is one of `everyone`/`roles`/`users`; `users` and `roles` are arrays of non-empty strings; `replied_user` is a boolean. Keep the refusal describing the TYPE, never the value, per the existing `typeName`/`figure` discipline. Also correct README line 75, or narrow it to the keys it actually covers.
testUpgrade: `config-values.test.ts`'s `REFUSED: Record<ConfigShape, Array<[string, unknown]>>` is already the right ratchet shape — it makes adding a shape without refusal rows a compile error. Add the `'mention scope'` rows as a matrix over (member x wrong type): parse as a bare string, parse as an array of numbers, parse carrying an unknown scope word, users/roles as a string, users as an array of numbers, replied_user as a string, replied_user as 0/1. Pair it with an ACCEPTED-values control that drives `post` end to end against the fake and asserts `fake.posts()[0].body.allowed_mentions` equals what was configured, so a validator that rejects everything cannot pass. The class the matrix guards is "a declared config key whose members reach the wire unvalidated", not the `parse` field.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `assertKnownConfigKeys('discord', config, CONFIG_KEYS)` (core), which already refuses a non-object and an undeclared member name under `nested` — so the new shape only has to grade member VALUES, not membership. Also `SHAPE_REFUSALS` being keyed by shape and dispatched in `assertKnownBackendConfig`'s loop, and `CONFIG_SHAPES ... satisfies Record<keyof Required<DiscordBackendConfig>, ConfigShape>`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `allowed_mentions: { parse: 'everyone' }`, `{ replied_user: 'yes' }`, `{ users: 5 }`, `{ parse: ['here'] }` — all of which load today and 400 at Discord on the first post.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: `config-values.test.ts` will fail to COMPILE (`typecheck:test`) the moment `'nested object'` is removed from the `ConfigShape` union, because `REFUSED` is a `Record<ConfigShape, …>` with a `'nested object'` key and no `'mention scope'` key. That is by design — the table's own doc says a new shape must bring values that must not load — but it means the fix is not a src-only edit. I grepped test/*.ts for other `allowed_mentions` config rows and found none; rest-contract.test.ts:995 only asserts `sent.body.allowed_mentions` is defined for the DEFAULT, which the fix does not touch.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the shape is added but only `parse` is graded, `replied_user: 'yes'` and a numeric `users` still reach the wire and still 400 every post — the bridge-up-but-mute symptom survives. Validating the shape does NOT narrow the blast radius of a deliberately wide-but-well-typed `{ parse: ['everyone'] }`; that remains the operator's documented choice, and nothing here should change it.

summary: The Discord conformance context omits `absentTopicBehaviour`, so `catch-up.ts:116` takes the `'empty-page'` default — but this plugin takes the `'throws'` arm (pager maps `10003 Unknown Channel` to `NoSuchTopicError`, and the README's "absent topic" row says so). The case only passes because `freshTopic()` calls `fake.createChannel(id)` first, making the topic PRESENT-but-empty rather than absent. The shared clause therefore grades Discord on an arm it does not implement, and the `'throws'` branch — which asserts the error NAME, its `.topic` field and that the message contains the topic — never executes for this backend.
failure: `packages/conformance/src/cases/catch-up.ts` 'fetchRecent on a never-posted topic returns an empty page with a replayable cursor' runs the `empty-page` branch for discord and passes; if the topic were genuinely absent (id never passed to `createChannel`) the same case would fail with a NoSuchTopicError rejection. So the one shared clause written to pin which arm a backend takes reports 'empty-page' for a backend that takes 'throws' — a silently wrong capability declaration that a future core change keyed on `absentTopicBehaviour` would read as authoritative.
remediation: Add an `absentTopic()` (or `neverProvisionedTopic()`) hook to `ConformanceContext` alongside `freshTopic()`, so the case can ask for a topic with no backend representation rather than inferring one from 'never posted to'. Then declare `absentTopicBehaviour: 'throws'` in discord's context and have `absentTopic()` mint a channel id without calling `fake.createChannel`. Backends whose topics need no provisioning return the same value from both hooks.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the shared case over the two axes it actually has — (topic provisioned / topic never provisioned) x (declared arm) — and make the DECLARED arm the thing under test: a context declaring 'throws' must reject with NoSuchTopicError on the unprovisioned topic AND return an empty replayable page on the provisioned-but-empty one. That makes a mis-declared flag a red for any backend, rather than a flag whose wrongness is invisible whenever `freshTopic` happens to provision. Add a suite-shape assertion in packages/conformance/test that every context supplying `absentTopic` exercises both branches.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `ConformanceContext.absentTopicBehaviour` (factory.ts:49) and its `CONTEXT_FIELDS` validator (factory.ts:67), plus `catch-up.ts:116`'s `(ctx.absentTopicBehaviour ?? 'empty-page') === 'throws'` branch. The discord side relies on `fake.createChannel` being what makes a channel resolvable (fake-discord.ts:345) — an id never passed to it answers `404 {code:10003}`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a backend whose declared arm disagrees with its observed behaviour on an unprovisioned topic — today that disagreement is unobservable for any backend whose freshTopic provisions.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Declaring `absentTopicBehaviour: 'throws'` WITHOUT the new hook breaks the suite immediately: `freshTopic()` provisions the channel, so `fetchRecent` resolves with an empty page and the 'throws' branch's `expect(err).toBeInstanceOf(Error)` fails. That is the trap in this remediation — the one-line flag fix is wrong on its own. Adding the hook also touches packages/conformance, which is a frozen shared package, so this is a cross-package change and needs the conformance owner, not a discord-local edit. packages/conformance/test/context-validation.test.ts asserts `optionalFields()` equals exactly ['absentTopicBehaviour'] and would need updating if the new hook is optional.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If only the flag is flipped and the hook is skipped, the case goes red and someone will revert the flag — leaving the mis-declaration in place. If only the hook is added and the flag left off, the clause still grades the wrong arm.

summary: The comment above `fetchRecent`'s budget derivation says the finiteness arm exists so that a budget "can neither reach a timer as `Infinity`, where it is a RangeError thrown out of the seam, nor hold the caller on the unbounded default". Node does not throw a RangeError there: `setTimeout(fn, Infinity)` emits a TimeoutOverflowWarning and fires at 1 ms (verified on this machine's Node). The named hazard does not exist, and the hazard that DOES exist on this path — a finite blockMs past Node's 32-bit timer range — is not guarded, even though `config.ts` exports `MAX_TIMER_MS` and refuses exactly that figure for `handshake_timeout_ms` and `gateway_dialers`.
failure: `plugin.fetchRecent({ topic, since, blockMs: 3_000_000_000 })` passes `Number.isFinite`, so `withDeadline(ensureUp(), 3e9)` and `arm(waiters, ch, ~3e9)` both arm timers that Node wraps to 1 ms. The call returns almost immediately with an empty page instead of blocking, and emits two TimeoutOverflowWarnings on stderr, polluting the operator log that `warn()` is otherwise careful to keep to one clean line per event. Not reachable through core (transport/tools.ts clamps block_ms to `catchup.block_max_ms`, itself capped at MAX_BLOCK_MS = 300_000), but the comment's own premise is that the seam "declares `blockMs?: number` with no bound".
remediation: Correct the comment to state what the arm actually buys (a non-finite budget would otherwise become `Infinity` at a timer and fire at 1 ms, and `NaN` would fail every comparison silently). summary: `DiscordSession` carries two `private get` accessors — `reconnectAttempts` and `heartbeats` — that forward to `this.gateway` and have NO reader anywhere in `src/`. failure: Dead production code that ships in the tarball and that a future reader must trace before daring to remove — and removing it turns two suites red for a reason that has nothing to do with the invariant they grade. Grade it on both sides with a synthetic fixture pair (a bare forwarder that must fire, and a forwarder that adapts or narrows, which must not). summary: Three defects in one 58-line file. (1) The module doc says the install "must carry the license the manifest declares" — `manifest` is parsed with a `license?: string` type and NEVER read; no assertion grades the license or `files`. (2) `emittedFrom`'s exclude machinery is unreachable: `tsconfig.json` declares no `exclude`, so `excluded` is always `[]` and the `matches()` helper — with its own regex-escaping logic — is never called. (3) `it('every already-built artifact in dist is publishable')` opens with `if (!existsSync(dist)) return`, so on any run that has not built (including this worktree, where `dist/` does not exist) it passes having asserted nothing, and `scripts/assert-no-skipped-tests.mjs` cannot see it because it is a green pass, not a skip.
failure: Deleting `"license": "MIT"` from packages/bridge-discord/package.json leaves this file — the one that claims to grade it — entirely green. Likewise, adding a `"exclude"` to tsconfig.json exercises `matches()` for the first time ever, with its regex-escape path never having been run. And `npx vitest run packages/bridge-discord/test/publish-hygiene.test.ts` on a clean checkout reports 2 passed while one of them ran zero assertions.

(b) Delete `matches`/`excluded` and read `include` instead, or keep them and add a synthetic-tsconfig case that exercises the exclude path on both sides. (c) Replace the `existsSync` early return with a build-or-fail: either run `tsc -b` in a beforeAll, or assert `existsSync(dist)` and let a local run fail loudly, so the assertion cannot be silently absent.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a test whose pass is indistinguishable from having run nothing" the way this package already guards it elsewhere: extend fixture-hygiene.test.ts's AST lints with a scan refusing a bare `return;` at statement depth 1 inside an `it()` callback that is not preceded by an assertion in the same block. Grade it on both sides (a guard-and-return with no prior expect must fire; a branch-specific return AFTER assertions, as in rest-contract.test.ts:442, must not). That is the same both-sides discipline the existing settlementFolds and inlineShapeCasts lints use, and it covers every future conditional skip rather than this one.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `manifest` already being parsed at line 17 with `license?: string; files?: string[]`, so (a) needs no new I/O. `packages/bridge-discord/LICENSE` exists on disk (confirmed by the file listing). CI runs `npm run build` before `npm test` (.github/workflows/ci.yml), so (c)'s hard assertion holds there.

I found no other test in the package that reads `dist/`, so nothing else changes.

summary: assertKnownBackendConfig type-checks only the members of `tls`; every top-level credential/addressing scalar (`token`, `user`, `pass`, `creds_file`, `nkey_seed`, `servers`) is passed to the driver with whatever type YAML produced. Its own doc-comment says a key this plugin does not read is a key it silently drops and that the guard exists so 'a misspelled token connects anonymously' is refused by name — but a mis-TYPED token is not refused at all, and `creds_file` reaches `readFileSync` where a number is a file descriptor.
failure: Reproduced three ways. (a) `backend_config: { token: 12345678 }` — the ordinary YAML spelling of an all-digit secret — is accepted by connect(); `connect({token: 12345678})` against my nats:2.10-alpine with NO auth configured fails with bare `NatsError: TIMEOUT`, naming neither `backend_config` nor `token`. Same for `pass: 123456`. (b) `backend_config: { creds_file: 3 }` reaches `readFileSync(3)` as an fd -> `Error: EAGAIN: resource temporarily unavailable, read` (verified through NatsPlugin.connect with the driver mocked). (c) `backend_config: { creds_file: 0 }` -> `readFileSync(0)` reads fd 0, which for `parley-nats` (an MCP stdio server) is the client's JSON-RPC pipe: verified that `readFileSync(0)` on an open pipe never returns (timeout exit 124), so connect() hangs forever AND consumes the JSON-RPC channel. `servers: 4222` and `nkey_seed: {a:1}` also sail through connect() unchallenged.
remediation: Extend `assertKnownBackendConfig` with a per-key declared-type check beside the existing nested one, using the same `typeName()` diagnostic and the same 'name the field, never the value' rule: `token`/`user`/`pass`/`creds_file`/`nkey_seed`/`subject_prefix`/`stream_prefix` must be strings when present; `servers` must be a string or an array of strings; `retention_days` keeps its existing numeric guard (which must still accept `null`). Do NOT special-case `creds_file` alone — the point is that the credential surface is typed as a whole.
testUpgrade: Class: 'a declared backend_config leaf holding the wrong TYPE'. `test/config.test.ts` already derives `declaredConfigPaths()` from the source and crosses a `NOT_A_STRING` table over them — but the loop is `paths.filter(p => p.includes('.'))`, i.e. nested members only. Widen it to ALL paths, with a per-path expected type derived from the interface text `declaredConfigPaths` already parses (string / number / string|string[]), asserting the rejection names the path and that `vi.mocked(connect)` was never called. Add `0`, `1`, `3` and `-1` to `NOT_A_STRING` specifically because `readFileSync` accepts a number as an fd, and add a case asserting connect() rejects rather than blocking (a bounded `Promise.race` against a timer) so the stdin-drain instance cannot regress into a hang that vitest reports only as a suite timeout.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `DECLARED.keys`/`DECLARED.nested` and the existing helpers in the same file — `typeName(value)` and `isPlainObject` — plus the existing nested branch `if (held === undefined || typeof held === 'string') continue;` as the model for the message shape. summary: The `retention_days` lower bound is graded only by rows generated FROM `MIN_RETENTION_DAYS` itself (`{days: MIN_RETENTION_DAYS}`, `{days: MIN_RETENTION_DAYS * 2}`, `{days: MIN_RETENTION_DAYS * (1 - 1e-12)}`) plus assertions that merely require 'some refused, some accepted' and int64-holdability. Nothing anywhere pins the floor to the ONE MINUTE the constant's doc-comment and the README both state, and docs.test.ts never reads the README's numeric bounds at all — so the registry derives its subject from the thing it audits.

Separately mutated the README's `It must be a number of days from \`1/1440\` (one minute)` to `\`1/60\` (twenty-four minutes)` and ran docs.test.ts: 198/198 PASSED. Concrete user-visible consequence of the undetected drift: an operator following the README writes `retention_days: 0.0007` (~1 minute) and connect() rejects it with an error quoting a floor the README does not state.

(1) In config.test.ts add ABSOLUTE low-boundary rows expressed in the unit the floor is stated in, not derived from the constant: `retention_days: 1/1440` accepted and composing `max_age = 60_000_000_000`, `retention_days: 59/86400` refused. (2) In docs.test.ts add the retention bounds to the existing claim registry, importing `MIN_RETENTION_DAYS` from `../src/config.js` and asserting the README's prose carries its printed form and the ~106751.99-day high figure computed from `2**63 / 86_400_000_000_000`.

Sweep the package for it rather than patching this one site — the same shape sits under `MAX_AGE_NS_LIMIT` (config.test re-declares `2 ** 63` locally, which is the right instinct) and under `MAX_STREAM_NAME_BYTES`. The durable form is a table `[{docPhrase, sourceExport, absoluteRow}]` where each row (a) asserts the README literal, (b) asserts the source export equals the literal recomputed independently in the test, and (c) exercises one input on each side of the bound written as an absolute quantity (seconds, bytes) rather than as `CONSTANT * k`. docs.test.ts's existing 'every extractor is probed against surfaces that exist' guard should be extended to require every registered numeric claim to have such a row, so a bound added later arrives ungraded-and-red rather than ungraded-and-green.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: docs.test.ts already reads the README (`README documents the real subject/stream names`, `the README's backend_config block documents \`${key}\``), so the file-reading half exists. config.test.ts already imports `MIN_RETENTION_DAYS` from `../src/config.js`, so the export is in scope. The absolute rows rely on `validateRetentionMaxAgeNs`'s `Math.round(days * NS_PER_DAY)` and on `fakeJetStream`'s `state.added?.max_age` capture, which the existing `retentions` table already uses.

remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None found — and here is where I looked. The new absolute rows sit alongside the existing `retentions` and `boundaryDays` tables and assert the same outcomes those tables already assert for the current constant, so at HEAD they are green. The docs.test.ts addition extends the claim registry, whose 'every extractor is probed against surfaces that exist' and 'finds the prose it is meant to police' guards would need the new extractor added to their probe list or they will report an unprobed extractor — that is the one place the change must be made in two spots.

summary: `streamNameFor`'s 255-byte JetStream name cap (and `validatePrefix`'s `maxComposedBytes`) correctly count UTF-8 BYTES, but every test that exercises the boundary builds its names from `rep = (n) => 'a'.repeat(n)` and `PROBE = 'topic'` — pure ASCII, where bytes and characters are the same number. The guard therefore cannot fail in the one direction it exists to catch.

So under the mutation a topic of 100 CJK characters (301 bytes) would pass `streamNameFor`, and the first `post`/`subscribe` would fail with that server error, which names neither the topic nor `stream_prefix` — exactly the diagnostic the guard was written to replace.

Add one server-gated live row at the accepted boundary for each alphabet, because the current 'accepted' rows short-circuit with `injectFake(...)` and never touch a server that has an opinion about the name — the fake models no length limit at all, so the accepted half of the boundary is graded by nothing. remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None found — and here is where I looked. config.test.ts's subject_prefix rows (`composes`/`illegal`/`empty token` tables) all use short values well under any plausible cap; the `prefix-live.test.ts` and `subject-live.test.ts` prefixes are `pw.`/`pt.<tag>.`-length. conformance.test.ts uses `pt.${tag}.`.

summary: isLoopbackHost parses the last IPv6 group with Number.parseInt(tail, 16), which stops at the '.' of an embedded IPv4 literal. summary: fetchOnce protects the abort side against Node's 32-bit timer with armableDelay (attempt.ts:92, 'cap, so that a budget past the timer's range is not wrapped into an abort one millisecond in'). The overDeadline guard passes because 2.5e9 < 3e9, so the loop reaches sleepUnlessStopped(2.5e9), Node warns TimeoutOverflowWarning and fires the timer at 1 ms. The lib comment claims the shared module exists so 'the preflight can never drift from what actually gets published'; the publisher imports only `publicWorkspaces` from it.
failure: Registry hiccup during the manual recovery path — which is precisely when this script runs, per its own header ('an automated release published only some packages (registry hiccup). Re-run this with that release's version'). `npm view @sharptrick/parley-core@0.9.1 version` times out; the script concludes absent and runs `npm publish -w @sharptrick/parley-core --provenance`; npm returns E403 'You cannot publish over the previously published versions'; execFileSync throws uncaught; the loop exits non-zero at the FIRST package and the remaining 12 are never attempted. The recovery tool for a partial release turns a transient network blip into a worse partial release, and reports it as a publish failure rather than as 'could not reach the registry'.
remediation: Import `registryStatus` from scripts/lib/workspaces.mjs in publish-workspaces.mjs and branch on all three values: 'present' → skip; 'absent' → publish; 'unknown' → abort with a distinct message naming the package and the registry error, since publishing on an unknown state is exactly the gamble the preflight refuses to take. Additionally wrap the `npm publish` call so a single failure records and continues to the next package, then exits non-zero with the full list — the whole premise of the script is idempotent completion of a partial release.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a decision made in two places where one copy handles the error case and the other conflates it with a normal answer. In packages/conformance/test/repo-contract.test.ts, add a parameterized case over every scripts/*.mjs that shells out to a network command (`npm view`, `npm publish`, `curl`, `gh`): assert the file contains no `catch` block that discards the error object without inspecting it, i.e. every catch on a network call must either rethrow or classify. Derive the network-command list by scanning for execFileSync/execSync/spawnSync argv[0] rather than listing script names, so a fourth script is a row the day it lands. Complementary and stronger: a planted-fixture case that runs publish-workspaces.mjs with a stub `npm` on PATH returning a non-E404 failure for `view`, asserting the script does NOT proceed to `publish` — nothing today would catch that, since publish-workspaces.mjs is referenced by 0 test files.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `registryStatus(name)` in scripts/lib/workspaces.mjs, specifically its `if (/E404|404|not found|is not in this registry/i.test(err)) return 'absent'` branch — I depend on that regex being the only path to 'absent'. summary: The keyed one-shot waiter parking lot — the primitive that makes a native blocking fetchRecent work — is hand-rolled six times, once per backend, with no shared implementation. Measured copies, each with the identical four-part shape (Map<key, Set<waiter>>; arm with a setTimeout; a fire path that clearTimeout + delete-self + drop-the-emptied-key; a teardown that snapshots and wakes all): packages/bridge-discord/src/waiters.ts:20 (45 lines), packages/bridge-telegram/src/waiters.ts:16 (56), packages/bridge-matrix/src/park.ts:88 (154), packages/bridge-slack/src/link.ts:152 (392, lines 152-190), packages/bridge-xmpp/src/archive.ts:201 (254), packages/bridge-postgres/src/state.ts + listen.ts. Diffing discord against telegram: identical control flow, opposite wake semantics (telegram gates `if (seq > w.sinceSeq)`, discord fires unconditionally), and two rewordings of the same risk comment about snapshotting the set before fan-out. bridge-core already owns the generic polling half (engine/blocking-fetch.ts) and bridge-net-util already exists as the place shared plugin machinery lives, so there is a home for this and it is not a seam violation — plugins depend on core.
failure: The concrete cost is measured, not hypothetical: this is the exact shape the review loop keeps re-finding per-backend ('arm the waiter AFTER the re-query and you reopen the gap you were closing' — four backends, four disguises). Because there is no shared primitive there is no shared test: packages/conformance/src/cases/blocking.ts grades the lost-wakeup window (it.each([0,1,2,3]) ms) for all ten backends, but the OTHER half of the parking-lot contract — 'disconnect() while a fetchRecent is parked returns bounded rather than hanging' — appears in no conformance case (grep of packages/conformance/src/cases/*.ts for 'disconnect' returns only live.ts's subscribe teardown), and is instead re-tested by hand in bridge-discord/test/disconnect-quiescence.test.ts, bridge-matrix/test/blocking-fetch-cleanup.fake.test.ts, bridge-slack/test/connection-lifecycle.test.ts, bridge-zulip/test/subscription-lifecycle.test.ts, bridge-postgres/test/waiters.test.ts and bridge-xmpp/test/pending-registry.test.ts. A backend that forgets its wakeAll() on teardown — bridge-telegram's Waiters.wakeAll() is called from exactly one site — hangs a caller's fetchRecent for its whole blockMs after disconnect, and the shared suite says nothing.
remediation: Extract the primitive into bridge-core (or bridge-net-util) as a small generic: `class WaiterLot<K> { park(key: K, blockMs: number, admit?: (w) => boolean): Promise<void>; wake(key: K, admit?): void; wakeAll(): void }`, with the self-clean, the snapshot-before-fan-out and the timer discipline written once. Each backend keeps only its own admission predicate (telegram's seq gate, matrix's (room, topic) key, slack's channel key), which is the part that genuinely differs. Then add the missing teardown clause to packages/conformance/src/cases/blocking.ts so the contract is graded at the seam for all ten backends rather than six times by hand.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a concurrency primitive re-implemented per backend, so its contract is graded per backend and each copy grades a different subset. Two ratchets, both class-level: (1) in packages/conformance/src/cases/blocking.ts, add a case guarded by ctx.supportsBlockingFetch that issues a fetchRecent with blockMs=5000, calls disconnect() ~50ms in, and asserts the fetch settles well under the budget — one case, ten backends, replacing six bespoke files; (2) in packages/conformance/test/repo-contract.test.ts, an it.each over every backend package asserting that no shipped source declares its own `Map<..., Set<...>>` of wake callbacks — i.e. that the parking lot is imported from the shared package rather than declared locally — derived by scanning src/**, so the eleventh backend cannot quietly hand-roll a seventh copy. The existing per-package teardown tests are too narrow to have prevented this: each one proves its own copy correct and says nothing about the class.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: packages/conformance/src/factory.ts's ConformanceContext (which already exposes `plugin` and a `closeServer`/teardown hook) and the `ctx.supportsBlockingFetch` capability flag that blocking.ts already branches on at line 43 — the new case reuses that same branch so a polling backend is not asked for native teardown semantics.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a backend whose disconnect() does not drain parked long-polls — bridge-telegram's single wakeAll() call site is the thinnest instance and is the one I would expect to be exercised first.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: The six bespoke teardown tests named above would all still pass (they assert the same property the new shared case asserts, so they become redundant rather than red — deleting them is the test-hygiene follow-up, not a breakage). The repo-wide scan in ratchet (2) would fail on all six packages until the extraction lands, which is the point; it must be added with the extraction, not before it.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Applied without the extraction, ratchet (1) alone still fixes the coverage hole — every backend's teardown gets graded at the seam. It hides nothing; if a backend hangs, the shared case names the backend.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The orderings the new case must survive: (a) disconnect lands between the plugin's re-query and its arm — the classic lost-wakeup window, already probed by the 0-3ms case for the post path and now for the teardown path; (b) disconnect lands while the waiter is armed and the timer pending — wakeAll must clear the timer, or the process holds an open handle past teardown; (c) two callers parked on the SAME key when disconnect fires — the shared wakeAll must snapshot the set before iterating, since each wake() deletes itself from the set and may drop the map key, which is exactly the mutation-during-iteration hazard five of the six copies each wrote their own comment about.

summary: `ensureRoom`'s failure handler evicts by KEY (`this.rooms.delete(key)`), not by identity. A rejection belonging to a retired generation therefore deletes whatever entry occupies that key now — including a successor written by the current generation.
failure: connect() [gen 1] → post('ops') starts `ensureRoom('ops')`, whose `POST /createRoom` is in flight. disconnect(); connect() [gen 2] → standDown() clears `rooms`. post('ops') → `ensureRoom('ops')` writes pending2, which resolves to `!room0:host`. Now gen 1's in-flight call fails (its token was dropped, so `http()` throws "refusing POST … no access token"), its `.catch` runs `this.rooms.delete('ops')` and removes gen 2's *resolved* entry. The next `post('ops')` re-runs `/directory/room/#parley_ops:host` and `POST /rooms/!room0/join` for a room already resolved and joined — wasted round-trips against the same homeserver budget the package works hard elsewhere to conserve, on every topic that had a write in flight across a reconnect.
remediation: Make the eviction a compare-and-delete: `const pending = this.resolveOrCreateRoom(...).catch((err) => { if (this.rooms.get(key) === pending) this.rooms.delete(key); throw err; });` — `pending` is assigned before any rejection can be observed, so the closure sees it. Same shape applies to `existingRoom`'s `this.rooms.set(key, Promise.resolve(roomId))` at line 151, which likewise overwrites unconditionally.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `standDown()` in park.ts:115 (`this.rooms.clear()`), which is what makes a superseded entry possible in the first place; and the fact that `ensureRoom` returns `pending` (the caught promise), so no caller holds the uncaught one. TDZ is not an issue: the `.catch` callback runs on a later microtask, after `const pending = …` has completed.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A `rooms` entry written by generation N now survives a rejection raised by generation N-1 for the same topic — one fewer alias lookup + join per affected topic per reconnect.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Nothing. In the single-generation case `this.rooms.get(key) === pending` is true, so the existing don't-poison-the-cache behaviour is unchanged.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I checked reconnect-lifecycle.fake.test.ts's "every internal registry is empty after a lifecycle that stood the loop down" (it asserts `rooms` is EMPTY after teardown, which compare-and-delete does not affect since standDown clears the map outright) and provisioning.fake.test.ts's "a read answers the same whether or not a write is provisioning beside it" rows (single generation, so the identity check passes and the entry is still evicted).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied and the underlying assumption were wrong — i.e. if some path DEPENDS on a stale rejection clearing a fresh entry — the fix would pin a bad roomId. I traced every writer of `this.rooms` (ensureRoom, existingRoom, standDown) and found none. What stays broken if not applied: only redundant homeserver round-trips; no correctness loss, since the re-resolve reaches the same room.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two callers on the new path: (a) two concurrent `ensureRoom(t)` in one generation — the second gets the cached `pending`, so only one `.catch` exists and the identity check is trivially true; (b) `existingRoom` overwriting the cell between `pending`'s rejection and the `.catch` running — the identity check then correctly declines to delete, which is the desired outcome.

summary: `MatrixPlugin extends MatrixParking extends MatrixTimeline extends MatrixSession` is a four-level chain of abstract classes with exactly one concrete implementation. It is not a hierarchy of abstractions — it is one ~900-line class split across four files, where `protected` is the only access control and every level reaches into every other's mutable state (`this.rooms`, `this.controllers`, `this.token`, `this.waiters`, `this.syncTimeoutMs`). The dependency does not point one way inside the package, which is the very property CLAUDE.md's prime directive asks for at the seam.
failure: No runtime failure — this is a shape finding, and I mark it PLAUSIBLE for that reason. Concretely: `MatrixPlugin.deliver` (index.ts:295) mutates `this.waiters`, which is declared and owned by `MatrixParking` two levels below and is only ever drained by `MatrixParking.blockingFetch` and `MatrixParking.standDown`; `MatrixSession.roomForRead` (session.ts:162) exists solely for `MatrixPlugin.fetchRecent` three levels above and is called by nothing in its own file; `MatrixParking.blockingFetch` reaches into `MatrixTimeline.driveBoundedSync`, `MatrixTimeline.fetchSince` and `MatrixSession.parkSlice`. A reader asking "who can invalidate `waiters`?" must read all four files, and a change to any protected field is unbounded within the package.
remediation: Convert the chain to composition: a `MatrixSession` object (baseUrl/token/generation/http/room resolution) constructed once and injected into a `MatrixTimeline` and a `MatrixParking`, each holding only the state it owns, with `MatrixPlugin` as the seam adapter that wires them. `waiters` then has one owner with a narrow interface (`park()`, `wakeRoomTopic()`, `drainAll()`), which is what `deliver()` should call.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing yet — I did not attempt the refactor. It would depend on `generation`/`stopped`/`token` becoming a single shared session object every collaborator reads through, since `isStale(generation)` is consulted in all four files.

summary: `args.since` is the one string in the read path never checked against the plugin's own ts grammar. Every vendor-supplied `ts` goes through `TS_RE`/`hasUsableTs`, but the caller's cursor is fed straight to `compareTs`, where `Number('garbage')` is NaN, `bySec` is NaN, `NaN !== 0` is true, and `compareTs` returns NaN. `aboveSince` is `NaN > 0` → false for EVERY entry, so the page filters to nothing, `newestSeenTs` stays undefined, and `emptyCursor` hands the same unusable cursor back. The topic is silently, permanently empty. This is reachable two ways: `parley_fetch_recent`'s `since` is `z.string().optional()` straight from the model (bridge-core/src/transport/tools.ts:97), and core's read-state loader keeps any non-empty string (bridge-core/src/engine/read-state.ts:41) — which is exactly the file this package's own README tells an operator to hand-edit to recover from `exceeded 2000 pages`. Core is already built for the plugin to THROW here: `fetchWithResumeHint` (bridge-core/src/engine/catchup.ts:98) wraps a first-page rejection with a 'that cursor was minted by a different backend, delete the state file' hint. Slack is the backend that answers silence instead.
failure: `plugin.fetchRecent({topic: 'C0PROBE', since: asCursor('garbage')})` on a channel holding messages 'a' and 'b' → `{messages: [], nextCursor: 'garbage'}`, and every subsequent call returns the same. Reproduced twice, including with the fake configured `setOldestWindow('ignored')` so the server returned both messages and the plugin discarded them. With `blockMs: 1500` and a live push landing at 200ms, the call parks for 1503ms and returns 0 messages, because `armWaiter`'s `compareTs(event.ts, 'garbage') > 0` is also NaN > 0.
remediation: Give `since` the same fail-fast treatment every vendor `ts` gets. In `SlackHistory.runFetch`, immediately after `const resumeAfterSince = args.since !== undefined;`, reject a cursor outside the grammar the plugin itself mints: `if (args.since !== undefined && !/^\d{1,12}(?:\.\d{1,12})?$/.test(String(args.since))) throw new Error(...)`. The regex must be the WIDENED one, not `TS_RE`: `emptyCursor` mints the suffix-less sentinel `asCursor('0')`, which `TS_RE` rejects. A throw is the right answer rather than a reset-to-tail, because core already renders it as an actionable operator message.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'a seam-supplied opaque value used in arithmetic without being held to the grammar this plugin mints'. Every `since` in the suite today is `'0'` or a ts the fake minted — verified by grepping every `asCursor(` site. Add a parameterized table over UNPARSEABLE cursors — `''`, `'garbage'`, `'1700000000'` (valid), `'0'` (valid), `'1e10'`, `'1700000000.'`, `'.000001'`, `'-1.0'`, `'NaN'`, `'store-7.42'` (a sibling backend's cursor), `'9'.repeat(13)+'.1'` — crossed with `{blockMs: 0, blockMs: 500}` and `{limit: 1, limit: 100}`, asserting for each that the call EITHER returns the true window OR rejects naming the cursor, and never returns an empty page whose `nextCursor` equals the input. Widen it further by making the conformance factory's cursor generator emit one adversarial cursor per run, so the class is graded on every backend rather than only here.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `emptyCursor` in src/messages.ts, which returns `args.since ?? asCursor('0')` — so `'0'` is a cursor this plugin mints and the guard must admit it; and core's `fetchWithResumeHint` catch arm in packages/bridge-core/src/engine/catchup.ts:98, quoted: `if (isNoSuchTopicError(err)) throw err; ... throw new Error('catch-up failed on topic ... while resuming from the stored cursor ...')` — a plain Error is wrapped with the operator hint rather than crashing the loop.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `fetchRecent({topic, since: asCursor('garbage')})` now rejects instead of returning an empty page; so does a cursor minted by a different backend, e.g. sqlite's `'store-7.42'`. Both were previously accepted and answered with silence.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None found. I applied the patch and ran the full package suite: 18 files / 1078 tests, all green. The narrow variant using `TS_RE` instead would break roughly every row that passes `since: asCursor('0')` — absent-topic.test.ts:58, blocking-fetch.test.ts:116/408/467/552/583, catchup-window.test.ts:126/225, connection-lifecycle.test.ts:91/159/273/277/282/328/375/413/708/715/804, conformance.test.ts:214, envelope-robustness.test.ts:173/497 — which is the trap in this remediation.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes. If the guard were added but `compareTs` still answered NaN for an unparseable operand, the only remaining exposure would be a cursor that passes the regex yet is outside Slack's real range — bounded, because the regex caps both sides at 12 digits, which is the same bound `TS_RE` keeps for the `new Date(seconds*1000)` normalize path.

summary: `renderMentions`'s fallback chain lets a poster choose the handle a message appears to mention. After `mention_map` misses, it emits `@${label}` from the attacker-supplied label of `<@ID|label>`, and failing that `@${id}` from the attacker-supplied body of `<@body>`. Neither is authenticated against `mention_map`, so any workspace principal that can put raw markup on the wire (any app/webhook/bot calling `chat.postMessage` without escaping — Slack escapes what a HUMAN types, not what an API caller sends) can synthesize a mention of any configured Parley handle and thereby defeat an operator's `live_push.mention_filter`, which is precisely the control that decides which untrusted messages reach an agent's context. The README states the opposite: 'an unmapped, unlabelled id surfaces as the bare id — visible, but it will not match a configured handle.'
failure: With `mention_map: {U0PARLEY: 'ctx-payments'}`, pushing `text: '<@U0EVIL|ctx-payments> hi'` from user `U0EVIL` yields `{content: '@ctx-payments hi', senderHandle: 'U0EVIL', mentions: ['ctx-payments']}`. `text: '<@ctx-payments> yo'` — an unmapped, unlabelled id — yields `mentions: ['ctx-payments']`, contradicting the README sentence verbatim. `<!subteam^Sxx|@ctx-payments>` does the same. All three reproduced on the live push path.
remediation: Keep the label/bare-id fallback, but never let it MINT a handle that `mention_map` has already assigned to a different Slack id: in `renderMentions`, after `mentionMap[id]` misses, return `raw` when the candidate handle (label or body, with a leading `@` stripped) appears in `Object.values(mentionMap)`. Then a configured handle can only be produced by the id the operator bound it to. Correct the README sentence in the same change — the bare-id fallback DOES match a configured handle today, and after the fix the accurate claim is 'a fallback never produces a handle you configured for someone else'.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'a field derived from untrusted inbound is treated by a downstream filter as an assertion of identity'. Add a parameterized table crossing the four markup shapes the plugin rewrites (`<@ID>`, `<@ID|label>`, `<!subteam^S…|@label>`, `<!here>`) with a spoof target drawn from three buckets — a handle configured in `mention_map`, a handle configured in core's allowlist but not in `mention_map`, and an unconfigured handle — asserting that the resulting `Message.mentions` contains a CONFIGURED handle only when the emitting Slack id is the one bound to it. Run the same rows through both delivery paths (history + live), since `mention-markup.test.ts` already establishes the two must agree.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `renderMentions`'s existing `const mapped = mentionMap[id]; if (mapped !== undefined) return `@${mapped}`;` branch stays first and unchanged, so the legitimate mapped path is untouched; and `MENTIONABLE_HANDLE` in src/config.ts, which already guarantees every `mention_map` VALUE is a handle core's parser round-trips, so `Object.values(mentionMap)` is a well-formed comparison set.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `<@U0OTHER|the-boss>` under `mention_map: {U0BOSS: 'the-boss'}` now surfaces verbatim as `<@U0OTHER|the-boss>` instead of as `@the-boss`. That is the intended narrowing, but it is a behaviour change for a workspace where a second account legitimately carries the same display label.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None found in the current suite — I checked every label used in the mention tables: vendor-markup.test.ts uses `mentionMap {U0BOSS:'the-boss', S0OPS:'ops-crew'}` with labels `boss`, `ops`, `general`, `the docs`; mention-markup.test.ts:210 binds its own MENTION_MAP. No row pairs a label with a mapped VALUE, so no existing assertion crosses the new guard. I did not run this patch, so treat that as a read of the tables rather than a green build.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Closes the mint-a-configured-handle path only. If applied while the underlying issue remains — that `mentions` is untrusted-derived and downstream treats it as authority — an attacker can still forge a mention of any handle the operator did NOT put in `mention_map`, which is the common case for a handle used only in `live_push.mention_filter`. The complete fix is either to require every filter-relevant handle to be in `mention_map`, or to stop letting inbound markup mint handles at all.

summary: `SocketModeLink.reconnect`'s single-owner guard is stated in its own JSDoc ('Keep this single-owner, so that a close arriving while a loop is already retrying cannot start a second loop: every loop dials apps.connections.open and their failures compound') and in the README ('only one such loop runs at a time'). Deleting `if (this.reconnecting) return;` leaves the ENTIRE package suite green — 18 files, 1078 tests — including the two rows written to grade it. They fail to grade it because `spyReconnect` counts INVOCATIONS of `reconnect()`, and each scenario loses exactly one socket, so `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` is satisfied whether or not the second caller would have been turned away. The flap rows, which do produce repeated losses, assert only a dial ceiling that a second loop does not breach against the in-process fake.
failure: Mutation applied and verified in the file, then `npx vitest run packages/bridge-slack` → `Test Files 18 passed (18) / Tests 1078 passed (1078)`. The two rows named 'an established socket dropped into <outage> keeps exactly one reconnect owner' and 'one reconnect owner survives the whole outage and resumes live delivery on recovery' both stay green with the guard deleted.
remediation: Grade the invariant where it lives rather than by counting calls in a single-loss scenario: assert CONCURRENT ownership. Drive two losses that overlap — drop the socket, and while the first loop is awaiting its cooldown (`dialCooldownUntil` is in the future, so the loop is inside `delay(cooling)`), drop again — then assert that only one loop is in flight. The observable is either the `reconnecting` flag read through the existing `internals()` probe (extend its return type, keeping the loud `expect(...).toBeDefined()` re-anchor), or a resolution-ordered ledger: instrument `reconnect` to push an entry on entry and pop on exit and assert the depth never exceeds 1.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'a concurrency invariant graded by how many times an entry point was CALLED rather than by how many are simultaneously in flight'. Parameterize over the ways a second reconnect can be requested while one is running — an established-socket close during the first loop's cooldown, a `disconnect: warning` envelope during it, and a blocking `fetchRecent` entering `ensurePollSocket` during it — and assert a max in-flight depth of 1 for each. The same table shape retires the identical hazard wherever a backend owns a redial loop: assert depth, never call count.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `internals(plugin)` in test/harness.ts, quoted: it already reaches `plugin.link` and returns `{waiters, reconnect}` with `expect(link, 'SlackPlugin no longer composes a link; re-anchor the internals probe').toBeDefined()` — so the re-anchoring discipline for reading a private is already established and the new read follows it.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — this is a test change, not a production change; it rejects no input, it only reddens on a mutation that today stays green.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None. The added assertion is strictly additional; the two existing rows keep their current assertions. I did not run the proposed test, so I have not confirmed the two-overlapping-losses scenario is schedulable against the in-process fake within the existing timeouts.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken today — the guard IS present in src. This closes the measurement gap, so the guard cannot be deleted in a later refactor without a red. If applied and the guard were later removed anyway, the new depth assertion is what would catch it.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The orderings the new test must cover: (a) loss A → loop starts → loop awaits `delay(cooling)` → loss B calls reconnect → second loop must be refused; (b) loss A → loop calls `ensureSocket()` → a `disconnect: warning` arrives on the OLD socket while that dial is in flight — `routeEnvelope` already gates on `this.reconnecting`, so the depth must still be 1; (c) two callers on the new path: a blocking `fetchRecent` in `ensurePollSocket` and the reconnect loop both hitting `ensureSocket` concurrently — they must share the one memoized `wsReady`, not open two sockets.

summary: The resume-after-`since` walk keeps memory at O(limit) by trimming `collected` to `limit + HISTORY_PAGE_LIMIT` after each page — the comment says so explicitly ('retaining only the oldest ~limit + page_size keeps memory at O(limit) while the walk runs'). Deleting the two-line trim keeps all 1078 tests green, because nothing in the suite observes heap. The bound is load-bearing against this package's own documented worst case: the README states a topic's backlog above its cursor may reach 2000 pages, i.e. 400 000 messages, and every one of them is retained as a `SlackMessage` object without the trim.
failure: Mutation applied and verified (`const retain = ...; if (collected.length > retain) collected.splice(...)` replaced with `void HISTORY_PAGE_LIMIT;`), then `npx vitest run packages/bridge-slack` → `Test Files 18 passed (18) / Tests 1078 passed (1078)`. Nothing distinguishes an O(limit) walk from an O(backlog) one.
remediation: Make the bound observable rather than only commented. Cheapest honest instrument: seed a backlog several multiples of `limit + HISTORY_PAGE_LIMIT` (the fake's `seed` already stages 5001 entries in conformance.test.ts) and assert a peak retained-array bound. Reading the private is fragile; a sturdier framing is to assert `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` growth across the walk stays under a multiple of `limit`, with the fixture sized so the untrimmed variant is an order of magnitude over — or to expose the peak retained count as a counter the walk bumps, and assert on that through the same loud-re-anchor probe pattern `parkedWaiters` uses.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'a resource bound the code states in a comment and no assertion can observe'. Parameterize over the seam arguments that drive retention — `limit` in {1, 100, MAX_FETCH_LIMIT} crossed with a backlog of {2x, 20x} `limit + HISTORY_PAGE_LIMIT` — and assert peak retention stays within a stated multiple of `limit`, so a walk that silently became O(backlog) reddens for every row. The same shape applies to any backend that pages a backlog newest-first and wants only the oldest window.

summary: The 'degraded event source must not withhold durable history' table asserts wall-clock bounds against a landing time it ASSUMES rather than observes: `setTimeout(() => fake.seed(topic, [{text:'durable'}]), landing)` with `landing = 0.9 * 4000 = 3600`, a budget of 4000, and only `SLACK_MS = 400` of margin. Under full-suite load the seed's own timer slips past the budget, the plugin's post-deadline read finds nothing, and the row fails on `expect(result.messages).toEqual(['durable'])`. Every one of the 30 rows in this table (10 degradations x 3 fractions) carries the same shape; the 0.9 rows are the ones with no margin left. The package README claims the suite is 'always green'.

The row passes 6/6 in isolation and passes under an 8-way CPU hog; only full-suite scheduling reproduces it.

Have the seed callback record `seededAt = Date.now()` and resolve a promise, then derive both `dueBy(seededAt - t0, blockMs)` and the 'cannot return before the message exists' floor from `seededAt`; and if `seededAt - t0 >= blockMs` (the seed slipped past the whole budget), the row has nothing to grade — skip rather than assert. summary: `blockForMessage` arms a waiter, then awaits the gap-closing `runFetch`. On the success paths the waiter is always released — `wake()` when messages arrive, `await wait` otherwise. On the REJECTION path it is not: the throw propagates out of `blockForMessage` and out of `fetchRecent`, leaving the waiter in `link.waiters` with a live timer, iterated by every live event on that channel until its rung expires. `harness.ts`'s `parkedWaiters` names exactly this class ('a waiter that outlives its call holds a live timer and is iterated by every later live event on that channel, and NOTHING else in the suite can observe either'), and every assertion built on it grades only the fulfilled path.
failure: Seed a channel, take its tail cursor, arm the fake to fail `conversations.history` from the SECOND hit onward (`onHit` + `failMethod`), then `fetchRecent({topic, since: tail, blockMs: 3000})`. The call rejects with `SlackApiError: Slack conversations.history → internal_error` and `parkedWaiters(plugin) === 1`, still 1 after a further 100ms. Reproduced.
remediation: Wrap the arm-and-requery in `try { ... } catch (e) { wake(); throw e; }`, or hoist the `wake` into a `finally` that runs on every exit from that iteration. The leak is bounded — the waiter's own `setTimeout(waiter.wake, ...)` clears it within one ladder rung, at most MAX_DIAL_BACKOFF_MS — so this is hygiene rather than an unbounded leak, but the registry's own stated contract is 'a settled fetchRecent leaves none'.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'a registration released on the success path and not on the failure path'. Parameterize the existing `parkedWaiters(plugin) === 0` assertion over CALL OUTCOME, not just over degradation: for each way the blocked call can end — normal arrival, deadline, disconnect mid-park, socket lost mid-park, and each way the re-query can reject (`ok:false`, non-JSON 200, a `SlackShapeError` on `messages`, a transport error) — assert the registry is empty once the call has settled EITHER WAY. The rejection rows are the ones absent today.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `armWaiter`'s `wake` closure in src/link.ts, quoted: `wake: () => { if (done) return; done = true; clearTimeout(timer); ... resolveWait(); }` — it is idempotent and self-cleaning, so calling it a second time from a catch arm after a successful `wake()` is a no-op. That is what makes a `finally` safe here.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — the rejection still propagates unchanged; only the registry entry and its timer are released earlier.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None found. I checked every `parkedWaiters` call site (blocking-fetch.test.ts:438 and the degraded table) — all of them run after a FULFILLED call, so an earlier release cannot move any of them. I did not apply the patch.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes. If applied while the bug remained — i.e. if the catch arm were placed outside the loop rather than around the arm/requery pair — a rejection from the FINAL post-deadline `runFetch` would still be uncovered, though that path arms no waiter, so it is not exposed.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The orderings that matter: (a) re-query rejects while a live event for this channel is mid-dispatch in `routeEnvelope` — the snapshot `[...waiting]` is already taken, so the stale waiter is woken once and then removed, harmless; (b) re-query rejects after `disconnect()` — `stop()` calls `drainWaiters()` then `waiters.clear()`, so the stale entry is already gone and the new `wake()` finds no set, which the `if (set !== undefined)` arm handles; (c) two callers on the new path — two blocked fetches on one channel, one rejecting and one still parked: the rejecting one's `wake` touches only its own waiter, since `set.delete(waiter)` is identity-keyed.

summary: CLAUDE.md is explicit that a comment earns its place only by warning a future developer off a risky action, phrased as 'keep X, so that Y', and that 'why an approach was chosen over another' belongs in the commit message. Several src comments are pure rejected-alternative rationale addressed to a reader rather than a risk warning. `compareTs`'s doc is the clearest: 'NOT a float compare: Number(...) loses the low-order digits outright once the seconds grow past the double's ~1 µs resolution there... NOT a lexical compare: seconds are unpadded, so 2.… would sort after 10.…' — two paragraphs arguing against alternatives nobody is about to take, for a function whose behaviour is already pinned by an 11-row vector table. `noteConnectionEnded` in link.ts:201 ('every one of its dials SUCCEEDS, so a ladder only failures advance is one it never climbs') and `HISTORY_PAGE_LIMIT` in api.ts:6 (vendor tier trivia) are the same shape. Across src the comment ratio is 476/1523 lines.
failure: src/messages.ts:63-68 is six lines of comparative rationale above a seven-line function. The risk it actually needs to state — 'keep the suffix compared as a fraction, so that .1 is 0.1 s not 1 µs' — is the last sentence, and it is the only one a future developer could act wrongly on; the rest re-argues a decision that `message-classification.test.ts`'s VECTORS table already enforces executably.

This is not durably guardable by a regex without producing a lint that can be talked out of a hit — the honest instrument is the existing source-scan file: add a row asserting a per-module comment-to-code ratio ceiling over `slackSourceModules()` (parameterized, so every module and every future module is covered and a new module cannot land above it), with the ceiling set at today's value so the trend can only go down. remediationCheck.reliesOn: `slackSourceModules()` in test/source-tree.ts, which already derives the module set from `tsconfig.json`'s `include` and throws when it enumerates fewer than two files — so a ratio lint built on it inherits the floor that keeps it from passing by scanning nothing.

summary: `ChatResolver.byTopic` (and `byName`) grow one permanent entry per distinct topic string a seam call names, with no bound and no eviction — removal happens only on rejection. This is the third caller-keyed map in the package, and the only unbounded one: `Diagnostics.callerKinds` is held to CALLER_KIND_MEMORY=256 and `ObservedStore.served` to SERVED_ID_MEMORY=1000, each with an inline rationale naming exactly this threat ("the topic space is caller-chosen — core's allowlist admits `post_topics` regex patterns").
failure: Traced. Core's allowlist admits post/fetch topics by regex pattern (packages/bridge-core/src/allowlist.ts, `postPatterns`, inputs up to MAX_MATCH_INPUT=64 chars). A config with `post_topics: ["-100\\d{13}"]` lets a model call `parley_fetch_recent` on unbounded distinct numeric topics. Each one takes the `NUMERIC_CHAT_ID` fast path (`Promise.resolve(BigInt(chat).toString())` — no network, so nothing rate-limits it), reaches `this.byTopic.set(t, pending)` and is never removed for the life of the connection, which for an MCP server is the life of the process. seam-driven-state.test.ts sweeps 2,500 resolvable topics and grades the store's durable exemptions and the diagnostics bound; it never measures the resolver, so this map is 2,500 entries deep at the end of a test whose whole subject is "a caller-chosen topic space leaves bounded state".
remediation: Two options. (a) Do not memoize the numeric fast path at all — `NUMERIC_CHAT_ID.test(chat)` is a pure function with no I/O, so the memo buys nothing there; keep `byTopic` only for entries that cost a `getChat`, and bound `byName` with a newest-last LRU. (b) Bound `byTopic`/`byName` with the same newest-last trim `ObservedStore.rememberServed` uses, sized well above any plausible `chat_map`. Option (a) is smaller and removes the growth at its source.
testUpgrade: The class is "a map keyed by a string the CALLER chose grows without bound". Extend seam-driven-state.test.ts's existing 'does not exempt more chats the more of them a caller names' two-sizes-an-order-of-magnitude-apart shape into a generic probe over every caller-keyed structure: after sweeping N and 10N distinct topics through each METHODS row, assert a measured proxy (process heapUsed delta after a forced GC, or a counted `getChat` re-resolution under a small cap) is not ten times larger. Anchor it on behaviour reachable through the seam rather than on a private field, so a map moved or renamed still grades.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `canonicalChatId`'s first branch, `if (NUMERIC_CHAT_ID.test(chat)) return Promise.resolve(BigInt(chat).toString());` — this is what makes option (a) safe to un-memoize. And `ObservedStore.serve`'s first line, `if (this.isServed(chatId)) return;`, which makes the `.then(serve)` side effect idempotent, so re-resolving a dropped memo does not append a duplicate `#served` line.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Not traced — I did not run this fix. The risk sits in chat-resolution.test.ts, which I did not read line by line and which very likely asserts a `@channelusername` costs exactly one `getChat`; under option (b) an LRU sized below a test's sweep would break it, and under option (a) the `@name` memo is untouched so it should not. Treat 'none found' as unverified here.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Applied, the growth stops. It does not change what a caller can reach — the store's chat cap and the served-mark bound already govern the durable side — so nothing else is affected. If applied while the bug remained (e.g. the bound added only to `byName`), the numeric path, which is the cheap and therefore the reachable one, would still grow.

summary: `append` asks `this.file.writable()` BEFORE `this.admit(...)`, justified by the comment "Ask for the descriptor before admitting, so that an unwritable store refuses the record without having evicted a chat to make room for it." Swapping the two lines leaves the entire 937-case suite green, so the invariant that protects unbackfillable history from being destroyed by a store that cannot write is coverage in name only.

Under the mutated ordering, with `observed_max_chats` reached and the append descriptor lost (a compaction that could not reopen the file, ENOSPC, EMFILE), every inbound message from a new unserved chat calls `evictLeastRecentUnserved()` — dropping another chat's ENTIRE retained history from the in-memory index — and then refuses the record anyway. The Bot API has no history endpoint, so that history is gone permanently, and `ingest` reports only 'the observed store has no append descriptor'.

Drive an `ObservedStore` to its chat cap with two chats' worth of records, force `file.writable()` false (the suite already knows how — store-compaction.test.ts and ingest-faults.test.ts make a compaction fail to reopen), then `append` a record for a third, unserved chat and assert that `entries()` for BOTH existing chats is unchanged AND the append returned `undefined`.

Parameterize one case over the refusal reasons `append` has — already-seen id, unwritable descriptor, every-retained-chat-is-served — crossed with the store's mutable state (`byChat` keys, `seen`, `evicted`, `nextSeq`, `evictedSinceRewrite`, on-disk byte length) and assert that a refusal leaves every one of them byte-identical to before the call. A new refusal reason then inherits the whole invariant instead of needing its own case.
